subsubtopic: FOOD AND HOUSING PRICE INCREASES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of the utmost urgency and gravity. It is the ever-accelerating rise in prices, particularly in the vital fields of food and housing, and the ever-present failure of the federal government, which has paramount responsibility in this area, to take steps to abate the current inflationary spiral and to deal adequately with the continuing rise in the cost of living. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens):
That this House urges the government to impose a temporary 90-day freeze on incomes, prices, rents and dividends, during which time it is instructed to meet with industrial, labour, provincial and consumer group leaders to formulate measures providing for medium and long term control of inflation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I request the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The matter concerns the fact that 600 students from nursery school to grade 8 inclusive have not attended school since Friday, May 4, on the Fort Alexander Indian reservation in Manitoba. Because of the deplorable conditions of existing educational facilities resulting in health hazards and illness, children at Fort Alexander are not able to receive the educational help which they so desperately need.
In view of the fact that this condition needs immediate attention, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development immediately take steps which will provide adequate educational facilities on the Fort Alexander Indian reservation.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 26 to propose a motion to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing an important matter requiring urgent consideration. I refer to the sharp rise in the cost of living, 6.6 per cent in the last year, the highest increase since 1951, which is particularly evident in the vital areas of shelter costs, up 6.9 per cent, and food at home, up 13.3 per cent, causing hardship to hundreds of thousands of Canadians, especially those on low and fixed incomes, and the complete failure of the government to alleviate this national crisis.

May 8, 1973
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John's East has filed with the Chair the required notice under the provisions of Standing Order 26 in which he seeks to move the adjournment of the House to discuss the question to which he has alluded. [DOT]
As has been frequently stated in considering proposed motions to adjourn the House, the question to be determined by the Chair does not necessarily concern itself with the importance of the topic but rather with the requirement that the matter should be one that should be given urgent consideration under the Standing Order. Obviously the subject is one of great concern to the House and to all hon. members, but in my view it is not acceptable at this time under the provisions of Standing Order 26. I would draw the attention of hon. members to paragraph 5 of Standing Order 26 which states in part:
In determining whether a matter should have urgent consideration, Mr. Speaker shall have regard ... to the probability of the matter being brought before the House within reasonable time by other means.
In passing, it should be stated that the question of the rising cost of living was covered in amendments in both the address and budget debates in this session. Additionally, as hon. members will recognize, the estimates of the departments concerned are still before committees. The question of rising food costs is now being considered by a special committee of the House. I might also refer to Bill C-133 dealing with the National Housing Act which is now before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
I am always reluctant to suggest that hon. members make use of the allotted days available to them under Standing Order 58 as I do not think it is the function of the Chair to direct the utilization of those days. On the other hand, I think I should remind hon. members that there are some 13 days available between now and June 30, and it does seem to me that some consideration might be given by hon. members to that aspect of our proceedings.
For these and other reasons, perhaps the form of the motion proposed by the hon. member which in some respects at least is more of a substantive motion or a censure motion, I would hesitate very much to suggest to the House that there should be a debate under the provisions of Standing Order 26. I regret I cannot put the motion at this time under the terms of Standing Order 26.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very much concerned that we should legalize a procedure which I do not think should be tolerated by the ordinary individual citizen. In the society in which we live we should seek to protect and ensure the right of the individual to free communication with other individuals, without the threat or risk of someone listening in on the conversations, and so far as I am concerned this includes law enforcement officers.
May 8, 1973

I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), when introducing this kind of legislation, should have fully protected the right of the individual to privacy within his or her home, or anywhere else for that matter. I believe that this bill should end at the proposed new section 178.11 which reads:
Every one who, by means of an electromagnetic, acoustic, mechanical or other device, wilfully intercepts a private communication is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for five years.
But I do not know whether the penalty should be that stiff. Along with my insistence on the right to privacy goes a dislike of putting people in jail for long periods of time. I do not believe that it does a person much good to be put in jail. I doubt that it improves his disposition, his attitude to society. The type of education that people get in jail is not to be recommended.
During the time which I have served in this House I have noticed that there is a great predilection on the part of ministers of justice, and I suppose on the part of those who advise them, to attach rather lengthy jail terms to the provisions of the various pieces of legislation which they introduce from time to time. I do not wonder that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has so much trouble with people escaping from jails, in effect walking out and leaving them. Surely, this should convince the Department of Justice that people do not like jails. If one could get this through the rather thick skulls of the people concerned, perhaps they would not put so many other people in jail.
As I say, I do not think we should introduce this type of legislation granting privileges or rights to police forces to use what are loosely called bugging devices, electromagnetic devices and so on, as super-snoops on the public generally. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), if these devices were really effective in the areas where they have already been used, crime would have decreased, but it did not decrease. If crime did not decrease under those circumstances, then what argument is there for using these devices? Undoubtedly, within the bureaucracy and among the perfectionists throughout our land there are significant numbers of people who would like to bring about a perfectly oriented society in which no one does any wrong. But such a thing hardly every comes into being. And when I look at some of the actions that have currently come to my notice I am not at all convinced of the infallibility of those who say they would protect us from malfeasance through the use of snooping devices.
Let me mention the matter of unemployment insurance benefits. I get many letters from people who have applied for these benefits. Now we have what are called benefit control officers. That description tells us something about our society and about the attitudes of government. They are not called inspectors or investigators, which would be good descriptive terms for the job they do. No, they are called benefit control officers. They are the men who work on benefits. I ask, for whose benefit? I get some letters about them. I could produce those letters but they are private. I have one here from a lady who says she did not really mean what apparently she said. She did not really want to incriminate herself to such an extent. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, she is in no danger of prosecution. The danger she faces is that she will be denied benefits to
Protection of Privacy
which she thought she was entitled, for otherwise she would not have applied for them.
Not too long ago I raised a question in this House about a labour dispute at a potash mine in my area, to which a member of the police force was sent in plain clothes. I asked the Solicitor General to investigate the matter. He did, and later he replied, in essence, that this sort of practice would not be continued. He did not give me a firm commitment that nothing like this would ever be done again, because I suppose he had to leave his officers the leeway they need. But there was a clear implication that in this case action had been taken which was not necessary. How do we know that people, officers of the Crown or police officers, who have these bugging devices in their hands and under their control, will not abuse them? It is my clear understanding that one party to a conversation can give permission for his end of it to be tapped. But what about the other party? Is he subject to the same procedure, even though he does not give permission? I would have thought the lawyers in this House would have been more critical of this legislation.
The Minister of Justice should examine his conscience pretty thoroughly when he brings this kind of legislation before us. This is the kind of legislation that can be used to suppress the rights of the individual; it is the kind of legislation that can be used to threaten people and it is the kind of legislation which has been used by dictators and authoritarian governments to enforce their will.
I recall at the time of the FLQ crisis in Quebec that the then minister of justice brought in follow-up legislation which made members of the FLQ subject to certain penalties under certain conditions. At that time I asked him how he defined a member of the FLQ but I did not get an answer then nor since, yet identification was crucial to the total approach. To my mind this was an infringement of the potential rights of the individual just as the legislation before us now will permit an infringement of the rights of the individual.
The pertinent clause of the bill, 178.15(1) reads:
Where the Attorney General of a province or the Solicitor General of Canada or an agent specially designated in writing for the purposes of this Section by the Attorney General of a province or the Solicitor General of Canada is satisfied that circumstances exist that would justify the giving of an authorization for the interception of private communications but the urgency of the situation requires that interceptions commence before an authorization could, with reasonable diligence, be obtained, he may, on such terms and conditions, if any, as he considers advisable, give a permit for the interception of private communications between persons, at a place and in a manner designated by him in the permit.
That is a wide open provision, Mr. Speaker. What is the urgency? At the very least this type of procedure should be hedged with the greatest possible protection for the rights of the individual, not left loose and open.

A minister does not receive too many plaudits or too many words of approbation. However, one subject that in this chamber must always be above reproach is the administration of justice. Without good judges, even though there are good lawyers before them, the citizen is not assured of justice at all times. Sir John A. Macdonald was asked on one occasion what he regarded as qualification for the bench. "Well", he said, "number one, that the individual be courteous and considerate and number two, if he knows some law I would not hold that against him". There is a great deal in that philosophy, because if you have a courteous judge who treats the young members of the bar with consideration it brings about an administration of justice that is respected. Of the appointments that have been made by the minister, it can be said that one of the qualifications has been the maintenance and preservation of that decorum on the part of judges that is characterized by courtesy.
I had no intention of speaking until this afternoon, but I was impressed this morning by an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail, which reads:
The wiretap bill to which the House of Commons addressed itself yesterday will not prevent a Watergate in Canada; but its swift passage would be an earnest that Canadian politicians set their faces against the moral corruption out of which a Watergate could grow.
I do not entirely agree with that. Under the parliamentary system, if we follow British traditions which, after

all, are the essence of parliament, I do not think there can ever be a Watergate in Canada. In the United States, and I am not in any way prejudging or saying anything that might be an unworthy observation, the division between the executive and the legislative makes possible what has taken place to the extent already revealed.
As a former prime minister, knowing something of the problems that arise in connection with security and also of producing, as it were, that political atmosphere that is necessary if one is to remain in office, I say without hesitation that nothing bordering remotely on what has been so far revealed in Watergate could happen under our system.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat dealt with this bill in a thoughtful way, but I do not agree with his thesis. I take exception to one section in this bill which I regard as dangerous to liberty and freedom within our country. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) has endeavoured to bring about a bill that will assure that degree of liberty that is necessary for free men, without permitting licence, too often mistaken for freedom, on the part of the individual. By and large I think it has been well done, with the exception of the section to which I will refer.
Before I come to that, I want to mention in general to the speeches which have been delivered in this House. I was not privileged to hear them yesterday, but I have read them. I have always made it a point to read Hansard thoroughly. I do not want to say that the other members did not make their contribution, but I am speaking particularly of the new members. The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) in his speech revealed a tremendous amount of research coupled with political acumen. I thought his speech was a pertinent and material speech. As I say, I did not hear it delivered, but from reading it I regard it as a very fine effort. The same applies to the hon. member for Halton (Mr. O'Connor) and to the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn). I read those speeches. Each, in turn, expressed a viewpoint. Each, in turn, has revealed, above everything, that there has been the fullest study given to the subject. I shall not deal with senior members who are present and have been members of other parliaments. I am restricting myself entirely to the new members, whose contribution did honour to them and to this House.

Having said that, I am concerned about a matter that affects all of us. No one who has not been prime minister has any idea of the responsibility that rests on the Prime Minister in the preservation and assurance of security, both within and without the nation. That is something that is with a prime minister at all times, even on vacation. That is something that he must constantly keep before him as he receives from day to day the secret and top secret ideas of those who are engaged in the administration of security.
Danger to the security of the state has been greatly multiplied in the last few years as a result of technological advances. Indeed, the United Nations' report dealing with this matter a few days ago said that some of the wiretapping devices are so small that they could be inserted into
May 8, 1973

teeth, hidden in flower pots and picture frames and even disguised as dogs' droppings. The report says that this kind of espionage erodes mankind's right to be left alone. An hon. member of senior distinction thought that this subject ought to be included in the Bill of Rights. However, speaking as one who had something to do, after years of advocacy, with the bringing in of that bill, I would not want to see the Bill of Rights have any such term within it.
The security of the state must at all times take priority over the rights of the individual, but at the same time the security of the state shall not be used as an excuse to unnecessarily erode and interfere with human rights. Espionage goes on. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made that clear in one of his rare appearances in the last few days before radio and television, and Canadian Press reported what he said. Yesterday, when he was asked about this by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell), he said that he made no charge. There is no suggestion that there was a charge in what he said. Let me read what Canadian Press reported. The reports reads:
Prime Minister Trudeau said Saturday he is certain Americans are spying on Canada but gave no hint that he believes illegal tactics are involved or that he is worried by the practice.
Probably, if we had the wherewithal, we'd be spying on them,' he said ...
What an amazing statement. I am sure the Americans have a lot of political intelligence on Canada. They cannot help but be disturbed since the Prime Minister's visit to the Soviet Union, when he told Kosygin and Brezhnev that we are afraid of the Americans, that we fear them culturally, economically and even militarily. That statement was understandable in so far as the first two items were concerned. The third part is something that no prime minister should ever have said regarding the one country in the world that today stands to preserve our freedom all over the world.

Where a permit for the interception of private communications is given under subsection (1) the person giving it shall in every case forthwith report thereon with full particulars to the Attorney General by whom he was designated for the purposes of this section or to the Solicitor General of Canada . . .

A permit for the interception of private communications given under subsection (1) remains valid, unless sooner revoked either by the person giving it or pursuant to subsection (2),

(a) for thirty-six hours from the time when it is given
Thirty-six hours! What an opportunity for snoopers to snoop. There is no need to go to a judge, though there are multitudes of judges available, but through an agent, and he can do the most terrifying things. I do not fear they would be done under the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) or under the present Solicitor General (Mr. AU-mand). I am not so sure about some predecessors of the Solicitor General. But this provision gives the power to destroy by snooping, the power to interrupt communications. And all that results is this: if he gets what he wants, well and good. If he does not, then nobody knows anything about it. In 36 hours you can raise a lot of hell under a clause like that, and I say to the minister in all seriousness: you have started out along the road to do something to preserve under law the rights of individuals. For goodness' sake do not, while on one hand preserving rights, undo all that is being attempted. In 36 hours you can do much to destroy an individual, and with all the force at my command I say to the minister: take this section out. It places the power in the hands of an individual to be designated, an unknown, an inconnu, giving him the right to do that which only a judge can do.
Why include this section? Have we run out of judges? The words are "when an emergency arises". Well, we have telephones today. It would not be very difficult to get hold of a judge. In this clause you destroy your whole objective and purpose. I am asking the minister to look into this because to my mind it is one of the most dangerous powers ever given by parliament, though at the same time in all the other clauses we are endeavouring to ensure that the kind of Watergating which went on in the United States shall be denied here by parliament.
Now, the bill goes on to say that the information cannot be used. You can snoop, you can listen, because you are an agent. You can listen and contemplate for 36 hours. But you can then forget about it. You cannot use the private communication unless the interception was lawfully made, and so on. But information obtained directly or indirectly as a result of information secured by interception of a private communication is not inadmissible. I do not particularly disagree with that clause. It is much the same as the provision that if a search is made under a search warrant, even if the search warrant is illegal, the evidence secured as a result becomes admissible in court. So, there is really nothing in that.
May I sum up, since I do not want to take more time than is necessary. As I say, that section worries me. It looks to me very much as though the person who drafted it thought to himself: "They will be blinded in parliament by what we are doing to make wiretapping legal, and they will give us power under the section to act as we will for 36 hours". I do not want my rights interfered with for 36 hours by an individual unknown and not responsible to parliament.
Hon. members know what has happened recently in the United States. Even making observations about it causes me very deep pain. The President has been a friend of mine for years. I wonder how many people in Canada who were going to abolish the monarchy are having second

thoughts now about asking for a president. The president occupies two positions. He is the head of state. He must have honour, otherwise he loses not only his national but his international prestige. Secondly, he is the head of a political party. He surrounded himself with a Praetorian guard that knew everything but honour. Certainly, I cannot believe he had any knowledge of recent events.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, where I began: what happened in the United States could not happen in Canada under our system where the executive is responsible directly to the legislature. How different it would be were the president not in the dual position under the circumstances that now exist in the United States.
I have nothing further to add. With all the sincerity that I can place before the minister I would ask him to withdraw section 178.15. It will be no retreat, no evacuation under fire, but rather a realization that this parliament must not be asked to place in the hands of an unknown the right to break for 36 hours every rule of the sacredness of the individual. Delete that section and we will have a bill that will, I think, become a model.
On the other hand, I also warn at this point that the United States has laws against wiretapping, which laws have now been proven to be ineffectual. Although not all of the dangers will be cleared up, we will at least show there is determination in this parliament to let Canada, the United States and other nations know that we shall not permit ourselves to take any steps toward a unified state and toward a superior bureaucracy that will determine the rights of individuals.

Mr. Speaker, one of the disadvantages in rising to take part in a debate that has reached the end is that much of your thunder has been stolen. Of course, when you have to follow one of the great thunderers of all times, then there is very little left for you to talk about. I listened with interest to the address of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), as I have listened to several addresses in the House on this bill, and I found I agreed with many of the points that have been made in terms of suggestions for amending the bill.
Thee is no doubt at all that as we look through the bill we are bound to find problems with it, but I am not going back over the ground already covered by my colleagues and other members who have asked for certain specific changes. Let me simply make one or two points about matters that I should like to see cleared up in the bill.
For example, section 178.11(2) provides:
Subsection (1) does not apply to
(a) a person who has the consent to intercept, express or
implied, of the originator of the private communication or of the
person intended by the originator thereof to receive it;-
The right hon. member for Prince Albert pointed out what he thought was a very dangerous section, and may I, in my own way, point out this other very dangerous section. For one thing, what is "consent implied"? I understand what "consent express" is, but I do not know what "consent implied" means. I have some knowledge of the English language and I have some knowledge of logic, but I cannot sort out just what that expression means. I concluded it must be a legal term, so I asked two lawyers

May 8, 1973
Protection of Privacy
today what it meant and they said they did not know what it meant either. There is an enormous difference in meaning between "implied" and "inferred". Is the inference of an acceptance going to be considered to be the same as the implication of an acceptance? Certainly, that is language that ought to be cleared up or perhaps simply removed.
Then a little further down in the sentence there is the little word "or" which is even more worrisome. The section provides that any party to a communication can give acceptance to the interception of that communication. In other words, I could phone up Mr. X and ask a person with bugging or wiretapping equipment to listen in on my conversation with Mr. X since I have, after all, given him permission. It is quite clear in this provision that I, as one of the participants in the communication, can give approval, and therefore what is done is totally and completely legal and not contrary to the act.
Again, it may be a matter of legal language which I fail to understand, but in so far as it is English I think I do understand it and I find it totally unacceptable. As a matter of fact, this confusion and difficulty is expanded in the same provision, where in subsection (3) it is provided:
Where a private communication is originated by more than one person or is intended by the originator thereof to be received by more than one person, a consent to the interception thereof by any one of such persons is sufficient for the purposes of paragraph (2)(a), subsection 178.16(1) and subsection 178.2(1).
So, Mr. Speaker, you can see the problem compounding itself. Any one person who is party to a multiple communication can give authority to tap the communication and to use the information thus derived for whatever purposes are legal, right and fitting. Surely that cannot be acceptable since at its worst it certainly could lead to framing, perhaps not a legal term but a term that most of us understand, at any rate. I could say to somebody else: "Look, I want to get Mr. Smith. I will call him, up, you listen in and he is bound to trip." After all, even Prime Ministers trip, as the right hon. member for Prince Albert said a while ago, so surely ordinary persons can trip. I could say: "Mr. Smith is bound to give us the kind of information we need to frame him". Surely, this part of the bill is not acceptable.
There are other sections of the bill which worry me. For example, in reference to something mentioned by the previous speaker, there is the question of agents of the attor-neys-general of the provinces or the Solicitor General of Canada. Section 178.15(1) reads:
Where the Attorney-General of a province or the Solicitor General of Canada or an agent specially designated in writing for the purposes of this section by the Attorney-General of a province or the Solicitor General of Canada is satisfied ...
How many agents will there be in all? Do we have any control? There are several attoneys general in Canada- ten I am sure-and there is at least one solicitor general. That is 11 persons who have the right without condition, without restraint and without control, to appoint agents. How many will there be? We have no idea. There is nothing in this bill to tell us how many there will be. There is nothing in this bill to tell us that there will be some control.

I shall not take up the point again at length that was made so effectively by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) yesterday concerning the definition of subversive activities. How in heaven's name do we define, with safety for the rights of the individual and his selfexpression, his liberty, his liberty of speech and action, what subversive activity is? We have never been able to do it. However, under this legislation the wording is there-if the attorney-general or the solicitor general feels there is subversive activity. There could, of course, be a cell of the Progressive Conservative party operating in my riding- which to me would be subversive-trying to subvert me as a Member of Parliament. How do we define it? The problem, I think, has been laid before the House and I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) will take this particular aspect into consideration.
My real point is this: The more I look at this bill the more I am concerned because there are so many parts of it which are questionable. The more I look at the whole question of wiretapping and the legalization for certain purposes of wiretapping, the more repugnant I am to give any support at all to this bill for the series of particular reasons to which I referred just now and the many reasons which have been adduced by other members of the House, but more important than that for the reason that I do not think the state should deliberately sanction this kind of activity within its borders. The state should not be involved in wiretapping.
It was a good number of years ago that the British Parliament threw out forever what was then known as "general search". We now have under our system the provision for search warrants, but search warrants are specific. A search warrant is issued to search the property of a certain specific person for a certain specific purpose at a specific time and with a specific end in view, all of which must be stated before the warrant is issued. Back in the bad old days there was a provision for general search. What the provision in respect of wiretapping on the part of the state, either for reasons of investigating criminal activities or investigating subversive activities, allows or, I should say, recreates, is the general search.
I shall quote here from a very worthwhile, extremely well written article by Stanley M. Beck entitled "Electronic Surveillance and the Administration of Criminal Justice".
These facts raise the vital issue in police use of electronic eavesdropping. It is that such listening is a return to the practice of the general search, a practice condemned and prohibited by the English courts in the eighteenth century.
It is not proper under our law to have general search, and so if we do not believe that a man's property or his belongings or his private household can be submitted to a general search then we cannot accept that his private life should be submitted to a general and continuing search under wiretapping. But, Mr. Speaker, in the case of general search, as bad as it was, it was usually one man's property, one man's household that was searched, not the households of many. When it comes to wiretapping you are searching continuously and generally everyone who communicates with the person that you are interested in searching specifically.
May 8, 1973

In order to give an idea of the application, I shall quote from a judgment of the United States Supreme Court because this judgment conveys some idea of how many other intrusions are involved, inadvertently usually, when a wire is tapped through electronic eavesdropping:
While tapping one telephone, police recorded conversations involving, at the other end, the Julliard School of Music, Broock -lyn Law School, Consolidated Radio Artists, Western Union, Mercantile Commercial Bank, several restaurants, a real estate company, a drug store, many attorneys, an importer, a dry cleaning establishment, a number of taverns, a garage, and the Prudential Insurance Company.
Of course, that is bound to happen. If you tap a telephone line and listen in on the conversations of people you will hear all kinds of conversations with people on subjects not at all related to the case in question because what you have done is re-institute the practice of the general search, a practice which was followed under the Star Chamber and which was thrown out two centuries ago. You have re-instituted it in a way and in a manner that the extremely authoritarian Star Chamber could not even have envisioned.
A while ago the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) stole some of my thunder by referring to a recent report of the United Nations on electronic eavesdropping. The report is not all that difficult to obtain. It was published in fairly large part in some of Canada's newspapers yesterday. What is described in this report is a mad and absurd world. It refers to listening devices the size of a pin, listening devices which can be inserted by a dentist in your cavity so that you can become a permanent transmitter of everything you say. It refers to listening devices that can pick up conversations miles away. There is a device which uses a laser beam. It can be focussed on your house and from a great number of miles away pick up everything that it is said. There are even madder projects. I shall refer to one which is humourous in a way, absurd in another and horrifying in another way.
A particularly ingenious device being used by various U.S. intelligence departments is an eavesdropping microphone which quite literally resembles a dog's droppings.
The device, intended for use in the jungles of Viet Nam, is also being used in the United States to gather domestic intelligence on extremist organizations.
The listening device is practically identical to the real thing, including the odour.
If I may interject, Mr. Speaker, what mind can conceive of such devices! Matthew Arnold once said that our most besetting danger is faith in machinery. This is faith in a certain kind of machinery gone absolutely wild. The article goes on to read:
It can be placed on a lawn near the house of whoever is being investigated, and its powerful transistorized transmitter relays conversations to a nearby monitoring station.
The gadget can transmit to a range of three miles and will remain operable for up to three months. It is weather-proof and flame-proof.
Here is where complete madness and the kind of mentality that would produce and use such devices begins to emerge. We were often told in the past that madness is logic carried to its absurd limit. Here it comes:
Protection of Privacy
The bug will often go undetected because of its unique form and the deliberate choice of this particular design is based in the natural reluctance to pick up such an object.
It is a mad world that produces these things, and I am not sure that we want to help in any way to create this mad world. It seems to me that the best way to make sure that no bugging is being done by private persons or organizations is to make as sure as possible that none of this equipment is around, and the best way to do that is to prohibit it completely because if you produce it for the police, for the armed services or for the state, it will be contrabanded and will find its way into the hands of individuals, criminals and spies.
So the only safe approach is a total prohibitionist one, and as the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) said so well, he would much prefer this act if it came to an end in its first clause which says very simply that it shall be a criminal offence to wiretap in this country, a criminal offence for everybody. I am sure that not too many people will agree with the absolutist position that I am taking. I know what the counter arguments will be. You need this type of thing if you are to protect yourself against organized crime.
Let us stop and look at that argument to see how much sense it makes. First of all, we are obviously not going to use bugging, are we, even if this bill is passed to trace down teenage marijuana smokers. By the way, there is no restriction in the bill-and I will come to that later- and no definition of the kind of crime for which the issuance of a permit would be justified. Let us stay for a moment with organized crime. There is much talk about it and relatively little definition. I return to Professor Beck. He says:
Organized crime is simply the application of corporate principles to the business of crime. It is sound economics and politics to aggregate human and physical resources into large organizations that provide central management and control, a division of labour, and prudent allocation of profits. In the United States, the Mafia or Cosa Nostra, is the monopolistic crime corporation. Its illegal activities are primarily supplying gambling, narcotics, women, money and liquor to willing customers.
It is important to realize that the basic business of organized crime is the provision of goods and services to customers who want them. We may not approve of their wanting them, but they want them. Professor Beck continues:
It is now said to be ploughing its huge profits into legitimate businesses.
It is just a different kind of business, more profitable and safer. Actually, it is a little bit more private because if you are in the Mafia you are being bugged all the time. Professor Beck continues:
All these crimes are, as noted above, crimes without victims, and for that reason are almost impossible to combat. All these crimes involve imposing someone's idea of morality on somebody who has a different idea. It is "coercion to virtue" through the law. If the criminal sanction is of little utility in these areas is it not time we stopped to ask exactly what functions the criminal sanction can perform, and which ones we really want it to perform?
In other words, if you are going to approach organized crime you have to review your entire thinking about crime and the kind of crime that organized crime is involved in performing. Professor Beck continues:

May 8, 1973
Protection of Privacy
Is it not particularly urgent that we ask this question if in the attempt to legislate morality we have spawned an infinitely worse evil-organized crime?
Even admitting quite clearly that we are not going to go through this deep philosophical review, we should at least be aware of one thing. If we are out to fight organized crime we have to be aware that organized crime cannot exist except where justice agencies dealing with criminals are not at least neutralized and probably corrupted to some degree. That is obvious. According to Professor Beck, organized crime is a large, well organized, well managed criminal business. You cannot operate this kind of large business without detection, and you are going to have detection if justice agencies are not neutralized, if they are active and not corrupted. Everywhere organized crime exists there is at least a strong suspicion, certainly the allegation and very often the fact, that the justice agencies are corrupted.
It seems to me that if you were out to fight organized crime, what you would do would be to restructure and reform the justice agencies that you have working for you. It has been proven time and time again that for all of its ingeniousness electronic eavesdropping is almost totally ineffective as an instrument of prosecution. There have been very few cases in which the direct evidence received through wiretapping has been used successfully in courts. I am not going to take the time of hon. members to cite the many reports that have been produced on this matter, particularly in the U.S., which has had a lot of experience with this type of activity. It is not a terribly effective way of obtaining information. Very often the evidence that is produced is not admissible in courts, so you cannot prosecute anyhow. All you have done has been to scare the rabbit, but you have not caught it. I do not know how many people here have spent part of their youth trying to catch rabbits, but I did and I know you only try once each time. It does not stick around for the second try.
So, what is the point of using all this marvellous gadge-try if it will not bring the effect you want, if it will not result in the effective prosecution of the criminal? All you have done has been to give him a warning. These devices are devilish and ingenious, but there are counter devices. You can bug a bug. It is hard to tell who is the bugee and who is the bugor. You can have a little instrument, Mr. Speaker, which can spoil the bugging. It is only a $10 job. Any high school kid can build an oscillator which will spoil any bugging gimick. So, it is not a terribly effective way of pursuing justice. But what it does is that it creates in this country, in this society, a state of affairs which is totally repugnant, a state of affairs where privacy for the indivdual no longer exists in any meaningful way.
I am sure that I am going to be told that certainly for the security of the state-as the right hon. member for Prince Albert said a while ago, and his was quite a statement- the security of the state overrides all the rights of all individuals. I might just like to add not all of the time and not in all cases, because there is a very large matter of interpretation involved here. However, for the security of the state, we can justify wiretapping. The situation is somewhat parallel to the attack on organized crime. Who are you going to tap? Of course, ideally you wiretap spies

to listen in on them. Well, if you are going to be very good at wiretapping spies no one will know about it, particularly the spies you are wiretapping as an act of counter espionage, and in the world of spies and counter spies legality does not obtain. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested, although he does not seem to be very well aware of the meaning of the word spy in French or in English, this goes on all the time. But one thing he is not aware of is that no spying is legal. Spying, by definition, is illegal. So here you are into an illegal realm anyhow, and if you are going to try to track down spies surely you will try to do it as cleverly and intelligently as you can.
But to.allow into the law the kind of provision proposed in this bill, to look into and listen into people's private lives on the grounds that they might be involved in subversive activities, goes a little too far. What we do, if we allow this, is that in this attempt to preserve what is called the security of the state we throw away what is valuable in our society. Let us ask ourselves are we willing, really willing, to bear this cost?
Let me see if I can make one more distinction which I think is very important, Mr. Speaker. People will say that in this matter I am a prohibitionist, and may say, "But look, what if the use of such a device could at one time save a life?" All right; fine. If you use such a device to save a life and prove to me afterwards that you saved a life by using it, I will say it was an extraordinary thing. I am not going to buy it as a general rule, but congratulations. You did the wrong thing, but you did it for a right and good cause.
But of course if you legislate this fact, then it is not simply a matter of saving a life. It almost becomes a matter of using the device to apprehend criminals. There is quite a difference between using a device to stop a killing and using it to apprehend a killer after the fact. Now, I am not going to go back over all the arguments to show that first of all it is not terribly effective, and secondly that it vitiates an extremely important principle of law, and therefore when we allow ourselves to use this kind of device it interferes with people's privacy. If at any time the government of this country was told by its agents that it had to permit a wiretap for the sake of the security of the country, then I would say that by specific act and specific decision, with full political responsibility, make that decision, and come back and explain to the country what it is you did, and why you did it. Mr. Speaker, we do this kind of thing in several other instances.
Many members in this chamber find the idea of telling a union that it members must return to work a repugnant idea. Certainly, my colleagues in this party find it repugnant in the extreme. Therefore, we will see no law which permits this on a continuing basis. If there is a strike going on which is causing so much harm to the people of Canada that it must be stopped, then we say let this parliament assemble and make that specific, extraordinary decision, because we want it to be just that, and have it known as an extraordinary decision. That is why we brought parliament back from summer recess in September, just to deal with that kind of situation. And when that happens we stand up, perhaps some of us with delight, but I know many of us with distaste and repugnance, and say to the workers, "You shall go back to
May 8, 1973

work." But what we have done on such occasions is that we have not only created a better situation by putting people back to work and removing distress from the country, but we have also underlined and sanctified the principle that there shall be no continuing legislation, no continuing law permitting people to be sent back to work against their will. I think the same kind of reasoning ought to be applied to this case.
I will end with one more point. It is a very general one, and it may be considered philosophical by members of the House. But surely it is not beyond some of us to be somewhat philosophical. Over the past few months we have been debating the matter of capital punishment. I have not yet had a chance to state my case in this House for the abolition of capital punishment, but I would simply want to say, when my time comes to state my case, that I respect the people who are opposed to my views, and I do not think for a moment that they support the restoration of capital punishment for vengence. Further, many of them will agree with me that the case for deterrence is not proven one way or another. There are facts on one side indicating that capital punishment deters, and facts on the other side indicating that it does not. The most powerful argument of those who favour capital punishment is that society chooses to indicate its abhorrence of certain crimes by inflicting the final, ultimate and absolute penalty. That is the only argument in favour of capital punishment that is worthwhile considering. And there is a counter argument. It is the one which I choose.
Admitting the value of the other argument I go on to say that society will not, by deliberate action of its own, behave in the same way as the criminal did. Society shall underline the value of human life by never taking it. And I add to this fundamental principle this utilitarian and practical point that if the state, within its society, creates an attitude of respect for life, then indeed this action on its part may reduce the level of violence in society, so there will be fewer crimes, fewer violent crimes, fewer killings and fewer murders, which is of course the objective of all those who participate in the debate on capital punishment, for or against.
Mr. Speaker, there is a parallel. If we in this parliament decide in full deliberation that we will permit wiretapping for certain utilitarian needs, for certain specific purposes, then we condone it. We would condone it but we would be much better to condemn it absolutely and have none of it, not for individuals, not for corporations, not for the police, not for the army-for none of us.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation before us has been introduced as a result of the state's duty to protect its secrets, information, institutions and policies against spying, carelessness, subversion and secret intervention. On the other hand, we are free to question the efficiency of the organizations and structures that the state has set up to carry out its responsibilities in an area in which the fundamental freedom of the individual may be at stake.
Protection of Privacy
In all countries, security practice involves a whole set of measures. There is an established procedure for classification, safe-keeping, handling and communicating documents and material that must be protected. This involves certain technical devices, and it is in this connection that some anxiousness has been expressed about encroachment by the state, and by individuals and organizations, upon what is commonly called "the right to privacy". This is a vast problem involving, for example, wire-tapping and the use of bugging devices, telephoto lenses, and certain other highly sophisticated devices used by the police and other bodies for detecting crime or for gathering information.
One related practice which seems to give rise to some anxiety is the use of certain technical procedures of investigation to obtain information. Of course, security measures applied, for example, to a staff of employees are an essential part of any efficient system. However, just as ordinary legal procedures can sometimes lead to injustices, so can security practices. Therefore, whatever provisions we draw up for the protection of individual rights, in the last resort, the individual's most important right, which consists in careful and fair treatment, will depend on the existence of a policy. Through that bill we now want to define that policy.
Mr. Speaker, the Official Secrets Act was a rigid piece of legislation written in broad and ambiguous terms. Legal cases which have already come up have indeed shown the haziness of that act and that it was rather lacking in precision and difficult to interpret. As stated in the report of the Royal Commission on Security in 1969 the revised act should protect unclassified information against any attempt at disclosing and gathering data which would be prejudiciable to the interests of the state or would be made with the intent to help a foreign power.
In recent years, people have been questioning the attitude of governments which maintained that administration activities and papers at their disposal should be kept confidential unless and until responsible authorities decide to make them public. However, this situation is much more complex and there are many exceptions, for example, papers dealing with national defense and foreign policy, personal departmental papers dealing with questions relating to social services as well as informal memoranda and drafts. In Canada, since there is no statutory provision other than the Official Secrets Act either forbidding or permitting access to government records, departments have had to treat individual applications on their merits.
Although the Royal Commission on Security recommends legislation in the area, it could not help adding, and I quote:
We would view suggestions for increased publicity with some alarm.
We think the knowledge that memoranda might be made public would have seriously inhibiting effect on the transaction of public business.
We believe that the process of policy-making implies a need for wide-ranging and tentative consideration of options, many of which it would be silly or undesirable to expose to the public gaze.
To insist that all such communications must be made public would appear to us likely to impede the discussive deliberation that is necessary for wise administration.

May 8, 1973
Protection of Privacy
In Canada, the bureaucracy is not vast, and the number of serious inquirers quite small.
It seems to us that there is no reason why controlled access to specific administrative files or documents cannot be permitted and arranged on an ad hoc basis when a genuine requirement can be established.
The bill now before us was prepared in the light of these wise recommandations, because the royal commission warned us of some dangers as regards technical security and security of communications; the commission used the following words, and I quote:
One aspect of physical security is generally referred to as technical security, and is concerned with protection against electronic eavesdropping and telephone interception, and with a variety of other technical subjects.
With regard to the security of governmental information transmitted by telegraphic means, we do not believe that there is sufficient awareness, even in senior governmental positions where it is most important, that the telephone is a basically insecure instrument, and that therefore classified matters should not be discussed on the telephone.
Therefore, we have prepared a relatively flexible legislation but also strict enough to meet the requirements of the security of the state while respecting as much as possible the individual rights to privacy.
To those who would be inclined to consider this new legislation still too severe as regards individual freedom against the security of the state, I shall answer the following: the high liberality of American legislation as regards the secrecy of state as often been praised but too much freedom in this area inevitably leads to abuses. And we can see today that the United States have to face the effects of such abuses, so that we do not know at present whether it is the president of the presidency itself that will be eliminated as a result of such a sharp problem.
Therefore, I suggest that we must be careful and forecast such abuses, by introducing an enlightened legislation.
This is why the bill now before us seems essential to me and I support it unreservedly under its present form.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-176 is entitled "Protection of Privacy Act". When I read the first paragraphs of the bill, I agreed fully with their content, but on reading the following paragraphs I agreed less and less to the extent that I for one shall surely be unable to vote for the bill unless it is amended.
The object of the bill, it would seem, is to protect the privacy of the citizens, or so its title claims. But study of the bill reveals-and I shall come back to its study clause by clause in a moment-that it will do exactly the opposite by allowing the state to do the contrary, that is to intrude legally upon the privacy of all citizens.
Before going on to the clause by clause study of the bill, let me refer to the statement the right hon. Prime Minister made in Toronto over the weekend to the effect that spying, through legal means, is allowed. Now it appears that what is illegal will be legalized: spying. To my mind, the state must not be authorized to spy-which is illegal- or to use legal means to do so.
Mr. Speaker, there is a social credit principle which we always put forward to the effect that we are in favour of freedom and the right of every citizen to freedom. Unfor-
tunately, this bill trespasses on the freedom of the individual, even when he is innocent, even if he did not commit any offences against the state or against anyone. I will come back in a while to the clauses which would lead to abuses, because as the bill is indefinite, we do not know where it will all end. We do not know where this bill will end. It is unfortunate that the present sad events which have been headlined for the last few days in the United States are being used, that the publicity psychosis is being used to move a bill which at first glance appears good, but which in practice is extremely bad for the freedom of the individual.
Mr. Speaker, this bill concerns me very much, and I only have to read the recommendation on page 2 which reads:
His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to the House of Commons the present measure to amend the Criminal Code, the Crown Liability Act and the Official Secrets Act respecting the protection of privacy: and to provide that the Crown shall, in certain circumstances, be liable for punitive damages in an amount not exceeding $5,000 .. .
Yet, Mr. Speaker, here we have the Department of Justice, which wants to establish justice in Canada, telling us that if this bill infringes on privacy, or that damages have to be paid by an individual because of the use of an electronic device or other under the present bill, then the state will not be liable for more than $5,000 regardless of the damages which could have been caused.
Therefore, in my opinion, this recommendation contains a clear and definite indication that this bill will be discriminatory against the people who will receive damages of $5,000, when in fact they will have suffered real damages of over $5,000.
That is the first reason, Mr. Speaker, why I cannot support this bill. Indeed, if the state causes damages estimated at $100,000 to an individual, and if we are to talk about justice here in this House, I do not see why the state should not pay for its own mistakes and misguided actions. It seems to me that an individual ought to be compensated for losses caused to him.
In committee, we will again consider the bill, clause by clause. Clause 178.12, as I read it, is in direct contradiction with the purpose of the bill. This clause gives complete freedom to the state or any of its agents. We do not yet know who these agents will be, but we may suppose that once again they will be officials who have never been elected by the people, and who will have the power to interfere as they see fit in the private lives of citizens.
Clause 178.12 states:
An application for an authorization shall be made ex parte
This means that when it is desired to search, bug, or wire-tap a private home, the application for leave to do so will be made ex parte, which means that the person concerned will not be present and cannot be represented. Authorization will be granted against him ex parte and in writing, without his permission, without the help of his lawyer, and even without his knowing about it. The application for an authorization must be made, and I again quote:
.. . to a judge of a superior court of criminal jurisdiction, or a

But who is the agent? Who is to appoint him? And how long will his term of office last?

. . . proceedings, if any, may be instituted at the instance of the government of Canada and conducted by. . . the Attorney general. . .
