speechtext:
that Bill C-23, to amend the Fisheries Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
Fishing Licences
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not often that legislation respecting fisheries comes before the House for consideration. This has been a rather busy day from the standpoint of our interest in fisheries. I have come, from a meeting of the Fisheries Committee on the Pacific Coast Fishery in order to proceed with the discussion of my bill to amend the Fisheries Act.
When the then minister of fisheries and forestry on April 20, 1970, introduced for second reading Bill C-204, an act to amend the Fisheries Act, he had this to say about the Fisheries Act:
It is an act which is as old as confederation itself. Our Fisheries Act was passed during Canada's first session of Parliament. It was passed more than 100 years ago.
He went on to say that the Fisheries Act has, of course, been revised and updated with the passage of time. The announced purpose of Bill C-204, the first major amending bill to the Fisheries Act which had been brought forward by the government for quite a period of time, was to make the Fisheries Act a more flexible and realistic instrument of law in relation to present day fishing methods in Canada and the proper conservation of the fishing resource.
An announced ancillary purpose of that bill was to tidy up some of the more archaic features of the act which had been left sitting over the years since confederation, since the first meeting of the parliament of Canada when the original act was passed. Certain changes along those lines were proposed by the government's amending bill. Incidentally, I may say that after very detailed examination by the committee, that bill was referred back to the House with very considerable changes from the original government draft bill. In my view, and I think in the view of members who were on the committee at that time, the bill was considerably improved.
On the matter of tidying up the bill and bringing it into line with twentieth century thinking, I proposed an amendment in the committee which would have involved deleting the present Section 7 of the act. After some discussion in the committee, my amendment was ruled out of order because it was beyond the scope of the amending bill inasmuch as Section 7 of the act was not opened up. As a consequence of that, and because I thought the matter I had tried to deal with was of some importance, I immediately introduced a private member's public bill which in substance sought to accomplish what I failed to accomplish in the committee. That bill appeared on the order paper in a position where it did not come up for debate. I have reintroduced it at each subsequent session since 1970. This is the first occasion when, through good fortune, it has reached a position on the order paper which gives me an opportunity to actually discuss it on second reading.
What does my bill propose to do? It deals with the matter of the licensing of fishermen in the commercial fishing industry. It seeks to eliminate what I consider to be a very archaic piece of wording in the present Fisheries Act. I am going to quote Section 7 of the act which I seek to delete. It reads:
The Minister may, in his absolute discretion,. . . issue . . . leases and licences for ... fishing,-

May 8, 1973
Fishing Licences
I do not know of any other piece of legislation which has that phrase in respect of conferring powers on a minister. To say that a minister in his absolute discretion may do something, in my view puts him beyond the normal reach of the control of the governor in council. It puts him beyond the normal reach of parliament and sets up a situation which is ideal for a dictatorial type of administration. That was my reasoning in 1970 when I tried to move this amendment in committee and it remains my reasoning to this day. Indeed, I feel that the events which have taken place since 1970 in the field of the administration of fisheries, with particular reference to this matter of fishing licences for commercial fishermen, have borne out the correctness of my argument at that time. The minister and his agents should not have complete discretionary power which is not spelled out by regulation. People should know where they stand. They should know what the rules are and they should at least know those rules cannot be changed without proper action by at least the governor in council. It is a field where regulatory authority is quite necessary and proper.
In the standing committee, I had this to say when I was arguing for my amendment. I quote:
Mr. Chairman, I think it should be obvious that the purport of my amendment is to create a situation where changes to licensing of fishermen or the issuance of leases can only be made under the authority of regulations passed by the Governor in Council. It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that an act which says that the Minister may, in his absolute discretion do something is really out of line with our understanding of our modern concept of the rule of law. Indeed, it strikes me that it is somewhat related to the concept of the divine right of kings and one would say shades of James I. I am sure the Minister is quite aware that this arises out of a situation that has developed in the last year or so on the Pacific Coast of Canada. The Minister has been changing the regulations as they affect salmon fishermen on the Pacific Coast by press releases. Quite apart from the merits or demerits of what the Minister has been doing, it has created a state of confusion. One day we have a proposal that such and such is going to happen under a certain phase of the Minister's program for changing the system of licensing and the next minute we have another press release issued from his office which says, "We are not going to do it quite this way but we are going to do it in this way".
I went on to argue a bit further for consideration of my amendment in the committee. The events that have taken place since that time in relation to the licensing of salmon fishermen on the west coast, the situation which has subsequently developed on the Atlantic coast in relation to the position of the salmon fishermen there and the kind of statements that have been made to me and many others by fishermen, indicate there is a growing disenchantment with the situation. The minister is allowed to exercise this completely dictatorial authority without any guidelines laid down so that a person can see in black and white under what terms and conditions he is or is not entitled to a licence to fish.
I am in agreement with many of the thrusts that the development of policy has taken under the present minister. With regard to some of the emphasis which has been placed on moves toward a new realm of a law of the sea, I give the minister some credit for the fact that Canada appears to be taking a much more vigorous stance than in the early sixties. It may be true that some improvement has taken place in the management of our fisheries and in the husbanding of our marine resources, but it seems to

me there is still lack of recognition of the fact that commercial fishermen are human beings and that they have a right to know where they stand in relation to the industry from which they make their livelihood; they ought not to have their livelihood taken away from them at the whim of the minister or of one of his agents in the field who might not be properly knowledgeable of the extent and purpose of certain aspects of fishery management.
The section of the act to which I have referred provides the minister with that kind of authority. It is an authority which, to the best of my knowledge, no other member of the government possesses. If anyone can cite another statute which contains the phrase that a minister may at his absolute discretion do this or that, I should like to know about it, because I have not been able to find it. That is why I welcome this opportunity to raise the matter formally by way of introducing a bill for second reading, and I hope hon. members will give it the kind of consideration I feel it deserves.
I might say in passing that clause two in my bill is somewhat redundant at the moment, though it was relevant when I originally introduced it. There was an oversight on my part inasmuch as the change I proposed has in fact been made in the Fisheries Act. This is a slight modification of the provision in the act which provides for the making of regulations. I believe that all the questions surrounding the issuing of such licenses should be laid out in black and white by way of regulations, changeable only by the formal action of the Governor in Council, and that the authority contained in this bill provides an adequate basis for rational arrangements to be developed in respect to the issuance of licenses or leases. In effect, the archaic section 7 of the act is redundant, unnecessary and unwarranted in the context of our present-day concept of democracy.

speakeroldname: Mr. William Rompkey (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ISSUANCE OF LEASES AND LICENSES IN ACCORDANCE WITH REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this amendment to the Fisheries Act seems, in my opinion, to be a retrograde step in the light of present-day requirements for living resource management and development both of inshore and off-shore fisheries. The issuing of licences still remains one of the most effective instruments available to provide for the development of sound management practices. It is becoming increasingly necessary in the light of the position we are taking at the Law of the Sea Conference and at various international agency meetings. Canada is presently taking the position that we should have control over the whole of the continental shelf surrounding our shores, 200 or 400 miles out, wherever it ends. As a matter of fact we are claiming control over the continental shelf to the end of the continental slope. If we are to retain credibility, not only among the nations of the world but with all sections of the industry within our own nation, we must display an adequate and reasonable measure of control and management of our fish stocks. We are looking ahead toward the management of these living resources on the continental shelves and this will require the introduction of new concepts in licence control.
Our renewable resources are among the most valuable we possess. Non-renewable resources have been disappear-
May 8, 1973

ing, but our renewable resources constitute a wealth upon which we can rely for many years to come and it thus behooves us to bring in measures for sound management control. We can only do this properly if fish stocks are wisely managed and protected. It is true to say that research into the fishery is more difficult than research into certain other aspects of our natural resources. For example, it is easy to see what is above the ground. It is easier to conduct research involving forestry or mining, as I think most scientists will agree, than it is to determine exactly what is happening beneath the surface of the sea. This is a further reason why more emphasis is placed on licensing.
Legislative jurisdiction over the fisheries of Canada is a federal responsibility under the terms of the British North America Act. This jurisdiction goes back from the Canadian parliament to the British parliament, because the resources of the sea are used not only by the host nation but by other nations of the world. Let me stress that the host nation, or the nation which possesses the resource off its shores must have control over the stocks and must have a preferential right in the fishery. It is for this reason we must ensure that licensing procedures are satisfactory. At the present time, under constitutional law, the federal parliament has exclusive legislative authority over the fisheries. This authority is exercised by the government in co-operation with the provinces, and in many provinces the regulations set out by the federal government are administered locally.
I indicated earlier the benefits which could result from sound management programs and I referred to licensing in this context, but such beneficial results, financial and otherwise, cannot be achieved unless the methodology of sound management is complete. Let me give hon. members an example. Our fishery stocks, because of the possibility of over-exploitation, demand very close monitoring in order to meet national and international commitments. Because of the tremendous strides made in fishing technology, it is quite possible for entire year classes of herring or salmon to be completely annihilated by a few non-conservation-minded fishermen who decide to disregard previously established quotas or fishing times. Most fishermen, I might add, respect the quotas and respect the regulations.
In my own province, most of the fishermen do not need to be told what the law is, or what the regulations are. Like others who live close to the sea, or to the soil, they are naturally conservationists; they do not really need to be regulated. On the other hand, there are some who do, and the threat of a rapid decline of stocks is so great that unless there is a control we can exercise at a moment's notice it may be too late. It might be said we should go through the process of appeal to the courts, or take action through committees. It may be too late to wait for that. We must have control that we can exercise quite speedily in order to ensure that stocks are not rapidly depleted.
If we were obliged to resort to long drawn out procedures we would, in effect, be doing nothing more than practising management on a retroactive basis. As I said before, we must ensure that we have that protection, that policing and licensing capability, the capability of taking
Fishing Licences
away a licence if something goes wrong in order to retain our credibility both with other fishing nations of the world as well as with the industry in this country. We are becoming more and more concerned with scientific management principles for many species, and the authority to issue leases and licences should not be restricted in any way. It is possible for a species to be decimated to the point of no return; therefore, the retention of section 7 is important.
The authority to issue licences provides a readily available and relatively simple control measure to regulate the size of the fishing fleet by regulating unit effort. It gives us the ability to control the entry of vessels and to control quotas and seasons. Licensing has also improved our awareness of the condition of the fishing fleet and the statistical information which forms a basic part for a sound management policy.
In addition to having and exercising control over our stocks, through licensing we can obtain additional information which helps us to employ sound management procedures. I have alluded to the other important aspects of licensing policy-that is, to regulate and control the entry of vessels, quotas and seasons, and to gather statistics so that we may be better informed and may modify our policies in light of the statistics we gather.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, there are now a number of restricted fisheries and, of necessity, there may be more in the future. The control of licensing is basic to the control of a restricted fishery. It is a simple, effective and readily adoptable method of regulating. No one wants to bring in these restrictions, but everyone will agree that you can only fish a resource to a certain point. There is a point of no return. There is a point where you deplete your resource so that it is no longer renewable. This is why we must have quotas.
From talking to people in my riding, people who have thought this thing out-and most of them do-I know they agree that there have to be quotas; they understand the reasons for them. Nobody likes them, particularly the people in my province, since for years they have become used to the freedom of access they have had to a number of renewable resources. For example, men might fish during the summertime a number of different species, as many of them still do, and then go into the woods in the wintertime to do some hunting or even to become loggers. They engage in a number of aspects of the exploitation of renewable resources, but I think all of them realize quotas have to be set and that licensing must be retained for this purpose.
The use of various types of gear is controllable by licensing. We issue licences for mesh size, for types of net, for total length of nets, for seasons, for seines, for trawls, for species, for areas and for many other reasons. The importance of licensing cannot be stressed too much, and it will be used increasingly in coming years as a control measure.
The conditions under which leases and licences are granted are continually changing. In this connection the fishing public demand immediate action. I made the point briefly previously that we should get to the stage where, if the law is broken, action must be taken right away. Or if we come across a similar situation to that which existed in

May 8, 1973
Fishing Licences
Placentia Bay, Newfoundland, a while ago, where we had high mercury or phosphorous content in the water, action must be taken right away to make sure the resource is protected from pollution of the environment. In this regard, it is very important that we have the proper licensing procedures to put a stop to serious situations such as these.
Let me for a moment visualize a situation where the Minister of Fisheries does not have the absolute authority to grant licences. I think that such a situation would place the minister in a very difficult position whenever occasion arose to cancel licences for flagrant infractions. I have previously discussed many such cases. The minister must be able to face a situation head on.
I am confident of the desirability of these policies in view of over-harvesting and the need to place the fishery in the hands of the real and genuine fishermen who depend on the fishery as a main source of livelihood. These measures have been effective and on the whole have been well received by the people whose main source of income is derived from fishing. Without the exclusive authority provided in section 7 of the Fisheries Act, these restrictive programs would not be sufficiently effective.
This amendment would raise doubt as to who exactly had the authority to grant licences. For example, if the minister is not to have authority, where would the authority lie? The bill proposes it revert to the Governor in Council. Does this mean, in effect, that cabinet would deal with licensing? Or does it mean the House of Commons would? Does it mean that a section of the department would issue licences? I think it is important that we know who does have authority, and that we know that this person can exercise the authority at a moment's notice if a serious situation requiring action were to develop.
With regard to revoking the authority to issue licences as provided in section 7, the proposed new paragraph (g) does not make it clear that anyone can issue licences. It seems to presuppose that someone can issue them, and indicates that the Governor in Council is empowered to deal in a general way with the terms and conditions under which licences and leases may be issued, without enabling the Governor in Council either to issue licences or to prescribe their actual terms and conditions. I do not think that ministerial discretion can be equated with arbitrary or unreasonable action, and the present paragraphs (f) and (g) appear adequate. A function as basic and general as the issuing of licences should not be left to regulation; its proper place is in the statute.
I agree that there should be some appeal procedures. I think people must have the right to appeal, and appeal committees have been set up already for certain species. Possibly they should be set up for other species as well. If a person loses his licence, he should have the right to appeal that loss and to justify his case. But we must be sure where authority lies and ensure that speedy action is taken if that is necessary.
There are a number of examples of where to illustrate the necessity for that authority in the past. I do not want to go into them at this time but I do think that if the authority were taken away from the minister this would be a restrictive step rather than a forward step. We have also seen that licensing has enabled us adequately to set
[Mr. Rompkey.j
regulations relating to vessels that are used to catch various species of fish. Nowadays, with the development of a multipurpose vessel, with men moving from lobsters to scallops to groundfish, there is still a large percentage following the historical and traditional way of life. It therefore became apparent that a restrictive-type policy would be a step forward towards harmonious development. A licensing program based on the authority invested by section 7 of the Fisheries Act was therefore introduced whereby vessels which had fished in excess of 100 traps became category "A" and could fish up to the maximum of 400. Vessels which had fished 100 traps or fewer became category "B" and could not fish more traps than previously. If a vessel had fished only 75 traps, not more than that number could be fished.
It was necessary to select the trap criterion because catch statistics were not available in the required precision. The catches may be sold over the rail, buyers may move amongst the fleet. We are moving toward a more realistic criterion based on catch value, but for the time being the described classification will prevail. Only category "A" vessels can be replaced or sold. Category "B" vessel licences are non-transferrable. When the present owner ceases fishing, the licence is gone except in the most extenuating circumstances to be determined by a review committee. Based on a licence control program for conservation reasons, a freeze was placed in 1970 on all herring fishing units with the exception of gillnets on the Atlantic coast. The policy stipulated that only those units such as purse seiners, weirs, traps, bar seines and midwater trawlers which fished in 1968 or 1969 would be licensed. Replacements can be made on a ton for ton basis with more extensive restriction in the Bay of Fundy area where overfishing became evident. There is inherent in this licensing policy a provision for entry into the fishery of additional units in all areas except in the Bay of Fundy where it can be clearly proven that herring are being produced for food and not for reduction purposes. The policy also provides for taking into consideration the status of the stocks.
To sum up my key points, I think modern fisheries resource management is based on quotas, restrictions of unit effort, area closures and gear restrictions. Decisions very often have to be made quickly, even on a day to day basis. To restrict the authority to implement management decisions by deleting provisions for licence control that now exist would serve to reduce and seriously impair the effectiveness of our management policies.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ISSUANCE OF LEASES AND LICENSES IN ACCORDANCE WITH REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make on this rather interesting bill that is before us. The question of licensing, of course, applies to any resource or privilege which is nationally owned and is not possessed as a matter of ownership by an individual. A farmer, for example, owns the land on which he carries on his operation. He is free, within limitations, to do whatever he likes because it is his property. However, in the realm of publicly owned benefits or assets which belong to the state in general, of course some system of licensing must be designed in order to determine how the resource or benefit shall be exploited. This is the reason it is
May 8, 1973

necessary to have licences allowing people to establish television and radio broadcasting stations. Only a limited number of people may exploit this resource or privilege which is owned by the state in general.
In the same way, the fisheries belong to the nation as a whole. Therefore, it is logical and indeed necessary in the present day that those who exploit this common resource should be licensed so that it may be determined to what extent and under what conditions certain individuals will have that privilege which in theory belongs to every citizen of the state. This, of course, is done through government.
If I understand the intent of the hon. member's bill, it has nothing to do with the abolition or the reduction of the necessity for licensing of the fisheries, because in this way and in this way only can exploitation of the fishery resource be carried on in a reasonable and beneficial way not only for the benefit of the people engaged in it but for the general benefit of the nation. Therefore, if my interpretation of the hon. member's purpose is correct, much of what the parliamentary secretary said is beside the point. I think what the hon. member who introduced the bill is attempting to do is not to reduce, restrict or abolish the issuance of licences or leases but, rather, to determine by regulation the conditions, the classes of people and the circumstances under which licences will be issued or cancelled. In other words, there would be a general framework in which the minister is required to operate when issuing licences. The explanatory note of the bill reads:
The purpose of this bill is to provide that leases and licences for a fishery or fishing shall be issued by the minister only on terms and conditions previously prescribed by regulations made by the governor in council and not in his absolute discretion as presently provided.
The section of the present act to which the hon. member takes exception is section 7. Section 9 of the act reads as follows:
The minister may cancel any lease or licence issued under the authority of this act, if he has ascertained that the operations under such licence were not conducted in conformity with its provisions.
This is a subsidiary authority given the minister to cancel licences which is almost as arbitrary as his authority to issue them, although he can cancel them only for cause. This brings me to a point which is of particular interest to lobster fishermen on the east coast where, I think due to the probably unnecessary arbitrary authority vested in the minister, the lobster fishermen have appealed to the minister and have asked him to cancel licences where regulations have been broken. This is a request which came from the fishermen. In those terms it is a very sensible and admirable request, because nobody should have the privilege of holding a licence unless he is prepared to live by the regulations. However, I think the application of the method of applying the subsidiary penalty for breaking a fisheries' regulation was not thought through sufficiently. I have reference to the breaking of a regulation, for which a fishermen is taken to court and fined under the standard system of justice which we all enjoy. This is fine.
However, we also have the additional penalty by which a fishermen forfeits his licence for a given period. I think this has been brought about because, due to economic
Fishing Licences
conditions, it was felt that the fines and penalties imposed by the courts were not adequate to deter the breaking of the law. I am all for clamping down on illegal fishing of any kind, so long as it is done justly and so long as the penalty fits the crime. But we have a situation involving a number of anomalies which I believe affects unjustly some individuals.
I might take the extreme case of a person who owns or acquires a few lobster traps but has no licence. He is an out-and-out poacher. He decides to catch lobsters. This also applies to skindivers who go out and catch lobsters while skindiving. If these people are caught, they are fined. They receive the usual penalty and that is the end of it because they have no licence to be cancelled. However, the situation is different in respect of the fisherman who tries to abide by the law, and most of them do. I might say there is a possibility of error if a person is out on a stormy day attempting to measure a lobster to see whether it is inside or outside the allowable size. Toward the end of the season it must be remembered-at least this is the case in my constituency-the majority of the lobsters are undersized and the fisherman has to throw them overboard. Sometimes he may make an error.
I should like to mention a case in my constituency. Last year a fishermen had a catch of 160 pounds. Fishermen are allowed 10 undersized lobsters for each 100 pounds of catch, but in this case the fishermen had a catch of 160 pounds which under the regulations would allow him to take a maximum of 16 undersized lobsters. It so happened that he had 19. He was taken into court and he pleaded guilty. This year he found that his licence was suspended for two weeks, which amounts to a quarter of the season. In my area this represents perhaps as much as 50 per cent of the catch and it means an economic penalty of around $3,000 on this individual for having three undersized lobsters too many.
It seems to me that the granting and suspension of licences is a very blunt instrument when used in that way. I agree with the parliamentary secretary that there should be some sort of local board which can give advice to the minister as to whether a licence should be suspended. When you have a lobster fisherman who is an unregenerate breaker of the regulations and who gets caught, you find that nobody has any sympathy for him. The feeling is that he had it coming to him. But when minor or borderline infractions of the law take place and it is a first offence, the suspension of a licence for an arbitrary two-week period is unjust.
I might add that in addition to his licence being suspended, the livelihood of his helper is taken away from him, a person who in all likelihood had no direct involvement in the infraction. I cite that case as a borderline case where I think the penalty was much too severe. It is over and above the ordinary penalty under the law, and one from which there is no effective appeal.
In this regard I have a great deal of sympathy for what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) has suggested, namely, the creation of a framework or some sort of terms of reference which should be adhered to in the granting, suspending or cancellation of licences of

May 8, 1973
Fishing Licences
fishermen. It seems to me that the granting of a licence to a fishermen is a privilege. It should be done in conformity with national interests in the broad sense and the protection of the resource; in fact, all the things to which the parliamentary secretary referred. Certainly the granting of licences must meet all these requirements in the public interest.
However, I think that what the hon. member is suggesting has merit. He is trying to ensure that situations where injustices are unintentionally perpetrated do not occur. I know that these things are done with the best intentions in the world, and I am not being critical of what the Department of Fisheries is trying to do. I am referring to unintended, but unreasonable punitive penalties imposed upon first offenders in borderline cases. Although the bill of the hon. member may be deficient and imperfect in many ways, I think that what he is trying to do has some merit.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ISSUANCE OF LEASES AND LICENSES IN ACCORDANCE WITH REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) for bringing Bill C-23 before the House. I believe it has a lot to recommend it. My understanding of the bill is the same as that of the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean), namely, that its intention is not in any way to decrease the necessity for careful management of this renewable resource or of conservation measures which we all agree must be strictly enforced, but to give more certainty to fishermen who prepare for the fishing season, probably at great expense, and who perhaps a few weeks before the season starts find that their licences are not issued for some reason.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni also objected to the minister having absolute discretion is this matter. He feels it would be better if regulations were made by order in council. The argument in the bill seems to boil down to allowing greater flexibility in the enforcement of regulations. If the decision were to be strictly up to the minister, this would be less cumbersome. However, I would point out that so far as I know, certain authority and discretion rests with the regional director of the Department of Fisheries to alter fishing season-to close the fishing season, in other words-when an emergency occurs such as the pollution of a river as a result of a spill, a flood or some other unexpected condition.
I know that this authority was exercised recently on the Miramichi River, in connection with the salmon fishing season, by the regional director of the Department of Fisheries in Halifax. In fact, it was exercised to the extent that he altered the season by two weeks. It had the effect of pretty well cutting the salmon fishing season in half. In spite of the fact that the regional office has used this authority, I contend that it was wrongly used in that case in 1971, and there is enough flexibility in the regulations under which regional offices operate in cases of sudden emergency.
Perhaps the question of seasons should have been included in this bill because it is closely related to the question of licensing. It is useless for a fisherman to obtain a licence, either from the Minister of Fisheries or through the authority of the governor in council, if some-

body else has the authority to cut the season or eliminate it altogether. Therefore the bill might have included some reference to seasons.
I think we all realize that in this very large country where there is an important fishery on the west coast, a very important fishery on the east coast, and the inland fisheries, there are too many details with respect to licensing and seasons for one minister to give them all his personal attention. If these matters were handled by order in council, other ministers of the Crown would be involved, possibly including ministers from the areas in question. In essence, I suppose this is an argument in favour of the bill.
If the minister undertakes licensing, as the present act says, at his "absolute discretion" he must rely on his own department; therefore he would rely on the regional office which has responsibility for the waters in question. I have had some experience with the Atlantic regional office in Halifax and I must say I would hate to leave the matter entirely in their hands. If the minister is unable personally to oversee these matters, then automatically it devolves upon him to look to his regional offices for advice on licensing and seasons.
I have given one example of where the regional office in Halifax cut the salmon season practically in half, apparently without any reference to the minister or to anyone else. I could give many more examples. Going back to the question of licensing, I can cite the present situation on the east coast where there is a commercial salmon fishing ban. About a year prior to the announcement of the ban, a policy statement was issued by the minister restricting licences and transfers of salmon fishing licences. It provided that to be a bona fide salmon fisherman or to obtain a salmon fishing licence you must not be engaged in any other industry, or not have a steady job in any other industry.
Many licences were cancelled as a result of this directive. However, in order to relieve hardship in certain cases the minister did agree that anyone, even though employed steadily, who was receiving a very small annual salary would not be considered to be steadily employed and therefore would be permitted to continue to hold a salmon licence. To deal with people who appealed on this basis he set up a licence review committee in the Atlantic provinces. It consisted of somebody from the Department of Fisheries, somebody representing fishermen and a third, independent citizen.
On the Miramichi, this committee set up by the minister to relieve hardship did in fact give relief in 13 cases. But the departmental officials from Halifax objected to the action of the licence review committee and, presumably, advised the minister. The result was that the minister upset the ruling of his own committee in nine out of the 13 cases. To me this is a matter of great regret. I only raise the matter to point out the insensitivity of regional offices, on the one hand, to the fishermen and apparently, on the other hand, to the wishes of the minister himself. So I would have to agree with and support the bill unless there is some way in which the minister can better control the actions of his regional directors and regional offices. I could give another example, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock, I was commenting Bill C-176, and particularly clause 178.12 which reads as follows:
An application for an authorization shall be made ex parte and in writing to a judge of a superior court of criminal jurisdiction..or an agent specially designated in writing for the purposes of this section . ..
What puzzles me, Mr. Speaker, is that we are still on second reading, and I suppose it will be possible to make amendments or clarifications to this bill, which is certainly in a good cause at face value, that being the protection of the individual's privacy. However, when we take the bill clause by clause, we see that its definitions are too comprehensive and not specific enough. Clause 178.12 a) says:
proceedings, if any, may be instituted at the instance of the Government of Canada and conducted by or on behalf of the Attorney General of Canada, or
And it says below that this can be done by a provincial Attorney General or by an agent.
The bill does not tell us who the agent will be,-and I should not like to draw any false conclusions-but I think it would be unfortunate to see some provinces appointing a political organizer of any sort.
Certain individuals will be authorized to install bugging and wire-tapping devices; if the agents are officials who, in some provinces, may be political organizers, this could lead to serious abuses and have even more dire consequences for individual privacy.
Mr. Speaker, clause 178.15 (1) also deserves our attention. This is another section that could lead to abuses. Clause 178.15 (3) says that it will be permitted to investigate for 36 hours before obtaining an authorization. It
Protection of Privacy
would be unfortunate to have people investigating, using electronic eavesdropping devices for 36 hours before obtaining authorization to install these devices. The legislation gives to anyone who has to use wiretapping 36 hours to get his permit or a writ from a judge, an attorney general, a substitute or an agent that we don't know yet; a citizen will be pestered for 36 hours before the person concerned may obtain a proper licence. I think that this is giving the legislation too much leeway and this might still result in most serious abuses.
On page 10, clause 178.18 (2), one may read about the exceptions:
(a) a police officer or police constable in possession of a device or component described in subsection (1) in the course of his employment;
Mr. Speaker, this bill is extremely serious; an authorization is given to all police officers in Canada. I would like to trust our police officers, but I think that the bill is too comprehensive and that we will unfortunately witness some breaches of confidence. Indeed, some individuals can enjoy pestering other persons in certain areas for all kinds of reasons. We see that police officers are ipso facto exempted under the legislation; they can, as they see fit, connect tapping devices on telephone lines or elsewhere. I think that this will give rise to much abuse.
The government is also empowered to use those devices or tapping apparatus as are police officers, authorized persons and officials.
I trust the members of the committee will amend this bill which, to my mind, is far too dangerous as it stands: limits must be set. If we do not want the bill to lend itself to abuse, we must amend it in several respects. At the present time, the bill could make spying legal, so to speak.
On the other hand, the bill limits to $5,000 only the punitive damages to be paid to the aggrieved person against whom wiretapping has been used abusively. As I said this afternoon, in every other field, when a person inflicts damages upon someone, in a car accident or otherwise, the law requires that individual to be penalized according to the damages he, in fact, inflicted; this is normal. This respects the spirit of justice. But in the case of wire-tapping, if an individual suffers damages worth $50,000 or $100,000, the legislation will prevent his obtaining damages exceeding $5,000.
In its present form, the bill was designed to protect privacy but actually, unless major amendments are made, it will place all Canadians at the mercy of government searches conducted by public servants. Each Canadian, Mr. Speaker, is entitled to privacy and the bill purports to protect privacy. However, it will allow government violation of privacy and pave the way to the creation of a police state in Canada.
It may be that the sponsors of this bill have no intention of creating a police state, but the bill will open doors and within a year there will be penetration of areas other than that of criminality and it is likely that in future the government, or National Revenue officials, taking advantage of new amendments, will use wire-tapping to achieve their ends.

May 8, 1973
Protection of Privacy
It is against such abuses that we do not want to see, and against the scope of this bill that we are protesting. I wish the government would propose amendments so that, in future, those who want to obtain search warrants or the authority to tap telephone lines would not be led to abuses. If this bill applied only to the field of organized crime and was only intended for the security of the state, we would be satisfied with it. Unfortunately, the people who will be called upon to enforce this act will be facing unlocked doors and we will see abuses such as the ones we deplore at present.
However, I have all confidence in the committee which will be considering this bill again. I hope it will be clarified further in the way suggested by the Police Chiefs Association, and by various other organizations which have at one time considered the previous bill, heard evidence in committee and made quite valuable recommendations. I will not say that the government has tried to bypass the recommendations of the various organizations in Canada, but I believe this is a new opportunity, when the bill comes before the committee, to propose the necessary amendments, in order to ensure maximum freedom to the individual, while allowing the government to use this instrument to control organized crime and to ensure the security of the state, rather than allowing them only to proceed with general searches and allowing officials and other persons exempted from the provisions of this bill, to make ill use of it.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to participate in a debate that, to judge from the speeches of hon. members who have already participated, is of significant value to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). I believe this type of issue is not partisan and the government is not so committed to its position that it will not show a degree of latitude in listening to, I will not say criticisms but constructive suggestions from members of all parties, including the government party. This debate will allow the minister to take a second look at the legislation. This measure has been before parliament on a number of occasions over a number of years; therefore we can end up with a very good piece of legislation that will be of use and benefit to the government and country in the days ahead.
First let me say that merely because we shall pass this bill in whatever form it may finally take does not mean that the law will provide real protection to the people of this nation. It will not protect us unless the government sees that the law is carried out completely and in every sense in the form in which it is passed. Provisions which allow for latitude in the use of wiretapping equipment in certain circumstances, or in the use of equipment that can reproduce sound, must be at all times implemented in the strictest sense so that those authorized to give permission for the carrying out of any form of surveillance which intrudes upon the privacy of any individual will provide to the public the greatest degree of protection possible.
There are a number of general things I wish to say. At present, in North America and throughout the free world, as a result of the Watergate scandal in the United States

we find ourselves in an environment in which we can fully appreciate the terrible consequences of misuse of the type of technology that is available today for invading the privacy of the individual. As Canadians we ought to be aware that it really does not make much difference if there are laws preventing the use of complicated computerized methods of invading privacy. If people and governments are determined to use these devices to invade the privacy of individuals, then the privacy of individuals will be invaded.
It is therefore the great responsibility of the Minister of Justice, whoever he may be, and of the Solicitor General, because he has control over and responsibility for most of the sources of producing information that may be required by the state in certain circumstances, to see that the right to privacy of the individual is guarded just as jealously as is humanly possible. I think that is the first lesson that we as Canadians must learn. Merely because laws are passed does not mean that those laws will be obeyed.
The second thing we must consider, and here we must depend to a great degree on the Minister of Justice, whoever he may be at the pertinent time, is that although the security of the state may be more important than the freedom of the individual, the Minister of Justice will need to be very careful in making sure that the security of the state is really endangered; in other words, he must be certain that it is endangered before contemplating action which will allow invasion of the privacy of the individual to take place. We, as Members of Parliament, must be careful that we do not allow in this legislation any degree of latitude to the Minister of Justice under which he might use his powers against an individual or group of individuals under the guise that he is doing so to protect the security of the state.
Also, in a parliament such as this we must be very concerned about the fact that there can be complication in the mind of the party in office in a minority government where the security of the state is mixed up with the security of the party which happens to form the government of the day. I especially want to emphasize this fact. The government of this day, the government of this country since 1968 has been, and has a record of being, a very secretive government. It has been very concerned about retaining as much information as possible about itself and making available to the public as little as possible of such information.
The government's jealousy about its own actions was one of the main reasons for the proliferation of leaks that occurred during the past two or three years. These leaks gave all Members of Parliament a great deal of concern. If they had happened too often and at too great a rate, there would have been a breakdown in the system of government as we know it and in the system of secrecy that must be expected from public servants, especially those who hold the highest offices in this country and who at all times should be subservient to the elected members of the cabinet or the executive who run this country.
I believe that Members of Parliament have shown real appreciation of what this legislation means. They have indicated real appreciation of what we should do to pro-
May 8, 1973	________________COMMONS DEBATES________________________3537
tect the right to privacy of the individual as well as what the security of the state means. As the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) pointed out in his speech, by initiating the constructive suggestions our party has made with regard to this legislation the people of Canada would have a right to know that is every bit as important as the right of the government to protect the security of the state.
There have not been many occasions when the present government and its predecessors have been willing to take the people of this country into their confidence and tell them what is happening. All too often we wrap up anything that appears to be the least bit political, anything that appears to have the least bit of political implication associated with it, no matter whether the public should know about it or not. We wrap it up and stamp it as classified, secret or top secret so that it can be kept away from the public. If a government becomes too jealous about this sort of thing, public servants are put in the position where they become the conscience of the nation. We do not have any right to put public servants in that position. Unfortunately, when we reach that point there is demoralization within the public service that is bad for any government, as well as for the people of this country.
If by this legislation and the approach the government takes to it there is an indication that we wish to protect the security of the state, protect the freedom of individuals and let the people of this country know what they want to know and should know, there will be an elimination or shrinking of the leaks which occur. There will be a degree of confidence, in the minds of Canadians, about parliament that will be truly beneficial to parliament and the parliamentary system of government.
When the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke today he said that the type of thing that has happened in the United States associated with the Watergate scandal could not happen in Canada. He should know a good deal more than I do because he was prime minister of this country for a long time. He had to deal with many top secret, security matters. He knows parliament better than anyone else in Canada and he knows what parliaments can do. He said that the Watergate scandal or something akin to it could not happen in Canada. I believe he must be right because I do not think there is a better man to make a judgment on that matter.
I say to the government that when we on this side of the House rise to ask questions which at times seem obnoxious to them, those who sit on the treasury benches should thank God that we have an opposition in this country. If it is an effective opposition, there is no way we will get into the kind of mess that today exists in the United States. That is very important. This is one of the reasons I have always been a strong proponent of a constitutional form of monarchy in this country.
We have a cabinet and an executive that is answerable in the House of Commons five days a week to the elected members who are here to ask questions. At times they may not like our questions. Maybe we ask some questions that get them into trouble. We hope so. However, we ask questions which we hope will show that the government of the day is honest in the efforts it is making on behalf of the Canadian people. That is really important. While we
Protection of Privacy
may be obnoxious, if we keep the government honest, if we eliminate the possibility of things like Watergate, then in the end we wind up with a much better system of government than any other which exists, even if it is not perfect or near perfect.
In recent days we have asked a great many questions of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) about the organization known as the security and research planning group. We have asked these questions, not because we are implying that some great, new spy network is being set up in Canada but in order to find out precisely what this organization is; and we are making these inquiries with a great deal of justification. When the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), who is sitting in the House now, was Solicitor General he enunciated certain aims and objectives for this organization which was known as the research planning group. The organization has now changed its name and has enlarged its scope. If we do not ask questions there is no way of finding out just what its area of responsibility might be. If we do not ask these questions we shall be failing in our duty as an opposition.
While the government appears to get uptight because we are asking these questions, all we are really saying to them is, "Tell the people of Canada what you are doing." As my hon. friend from Fundy-Royal said, Canadians have a right to know. I say that any police organization set up in this country which enlarges its responsibility over a two-year period, changes its name, adds people to its staff and says it will make judgments on classified information and train people for security positions in the organization or in government, is a legitimate target of inquiry.
I do not say there is anything wrong with this organization, but I do say that people have a right to know what it is all about. Yet every time a question is asked on this subject, government spokesmen give the opposition and the people a lot of double-talk, and the minute people hear double-talk they begin to be worried lest there is something going on that the government does not wish them to know about. It is the responsibility of any party in opposition, especially when it comes to the setting up of a new type of police force, to see that the people know everything about that police force, because such a police force might be invading the privacy of Canadians in one way or another.
If it is doing so, the people have a right to know why it is being done. We in the opposition intend to make sure they have all the information which can possibly be secured, regardless of how it is obtained, whether by placing questions on the order paper, through making speeches in the House or by asking questions orally during the question period. It is the right and the duty of all members of the opposition to see that the facts are placed before the people as clearly as possible. Certainly, as a member of the House I intend to see that those facts are made available.
I should like to return now to an aspect to which I referred earlier. It is one thing to pass a law and it is quite another to see that people respect it. If people are to respect the law, then the government has to set an example. The government has to see that for its part the law is

May 8, 1973
Protection of Privacy
carried out to the letter. From this point of view I should like to refer to the legislation which presently stands on the statute books with regard to the trial period for the abolition of capital punishment except in certain specific circumstances. I sat through the debate in the House when this legislation was passed. I had formerly been a reten-tionist, but I accepted what the government was saying and agreed to support the legislation for the five-year trial period which was proposed.
I was deceived, just as every other member of this chamber who supported that legislation in similar circumstances was deceived. The government did not live by the law. It lived by its own conscience. It paid no attention to parliament. It made a mockery of the law because it declined to carry out the terms of the legislation. Since that time there has been a rapid deterioration in all aspects of justice in this country. A question was answered in the House recently in relation to the number of escapes from penal institutions. Here are some statistics in that regard. In 1968 there were 108 escapes, in 1969 there were 174, in 1970 there were 293, in 1971 there were 485, and in 1972 there were 684.
Mr. Speaker, if this continues we shall have more prisoners outside the institutions than in them, and we shall be hiring more guards than there are inmates. As a matter of fact, that is almost the situation at the present time. This is just one example of the way in which all aspects of criminal law have deteriorated. This is because the government, for reasons best known to itself, would not live up to the law which was passed by parliament. Yet they have the outstanding nerve to come here and ask us to continue the five-year trial period in connection with a piece of legislation which was never put into effect in the first place. There are many examples of the deterioration to which I have referred. I believe the right hon. member for Prince Albert was right today when he said to the Solicitor General that we must have a royal commission, an over-all inquiry carried out as soon as possible.
I have in my hand information about an inmate in a penal institution who was sentenced to 18 months for trafficking in a controlled drug. This individual was a correctional officer at a penal institution and was trafficking in a controlled drug in the institution. In other words, he was trafficking in a drug in a most despicable way because he was selling the drug to inmates of a penal institution. He broke his trust as a correctional officer and endangered the lives of all his fellow correctional officers in the institution, as well as many of the inmates. He was sentenced to 18 months, and served only 27 days in jail before he was allowed out to work. We cannot have that kind of justice in this country. We must put justice back on the rails or there will be no justice in Canada.
I do not know whether I have used up all my time, Mr. Speaker, but may I just say this. I believe that the legislation proposed is very important. I believe the House of Commons has approached the legislation in a considered, non-partisan manner in the hope that we will arrive at the best possible legislation dealing with one of the most delicate matters that exists in this or any other nation. I believe the Minister of Justice is the kind of minister who will give every possible consideration to all criticisms that

have been made or that will be made during the committee stage. In the end I think we will have a good statute.
Nevertheless, it will only be as good as the government makes it by honouring the law that is passed. There are many dictatorships in the world with constitutions as fancy as words can produce and granting all kinds of freedoms, whereas in fact no freedom at all exists in the country. After we have put these words together and arrived at the best possible legislation, the Minister of Justice will have the grave responsibility of seeing that the legislation is honoured in every sense of that word.
If that is the case, then there will be protection for the individual in this country. There will be protection for the state and there will be a degree of justice in Canada of which we can be proud. We shall always be able to hold our heads high with legislation such as this under our system of government and we will not be concerned with the kind of international embarrassment which the United States is facing at the present time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin my short closing remarks by expressing my appreciation to hon. members of the House for their participation in this debate. If I may do so without presumption, may I also express my appreciation of their analysis of certain key areas of the bill before us which I know will receive further and serious consideration in the committee.
It is true, as the hon. member for Cumberland-Colches-ter North (Mr. Coates) has just said, that much of the approach has been in a non-partisan manner, since certainly members within the same party have not always necessarily agreed upon the exact approach that should be taken. I think this has been typical in the discussion of this matter initially in committee, in the House and in committee last year when the same subject matter, essentially the same bill, was before the House.
The main thrust, the key and central portion of this bill is an attempt to increase the protection of privacy in Canada by making illegal in a general way the use of a whole series of devices, particularly mechanical and electrical devices, that can intercept conversations of people who do not want them to be intercepted. As I see it, this key, central part of the bill has received general support.
I think it is worth noting that the placing in the hands of law enforcement officers, upon whom we depend for the effective operation of this legislation, the power to attempt to control the use of such devices strengthens their position; indeed, we are also making it illegal to have in one's possession or to sell, except in certain limited ways, such devices. This controlling of possession and of sale is one of the effective ways of limiting the availability of these devices in the country, except when those devices are used in an authorized manner.
It has been said by a number of hon. members that making wiretapping or interference with privacy illegal does not by any means completely put us out of the danger that it will continue in an unauthorized and illegal manner. Indeed, it is interesting to note that one or two
May 8, 1973

members commented that it is not the making illegal of such practices that will protect us as parliamentarians, as members of a democratic society, from the use of such devices in the democratic process. I am sure all hon. members would agree that none of us in this House would have tolerated the use of these devices by one of us upon the other, even during the period when there was no illegality. But this would be on the basis of our political ethic rather than on the basis of the law itself. It is that political ethic, that standard of conduct that we have come to expect from members participating in the democratic process which is by far our greatest protection.
A great protection also exists in our democratic process in the quality and the ability of our enforcement officers and in the way in which they go about the business of attempting, on our behalf, to protect us in a general way by maintaining law and order under the direction of the political authority which must take the responsibility for their actions in enforcing the law. I shall say a little more about that later.
My point is that making wiretapping illegal does not necessarily end it entirely. I think it would be a safe prediction to say that those elements engaged in the most serious crimes, the most organized elements of the criminal world, are still apt to make use of such devices even though use of those devices will be illegal. In other words when, in my hypothesis, these people are engaged in criminal activity, they will use these devices notwithstanding this change in the law. Thus, it will be important for our enforcement officers to attempt to come to grips with this problem, and here again we will rely on the quality of our enforcement officers, subject of course, as I say, to the responsibility of the political officers under whom they operate.
For this reason it is extremely important that in the committee we face up to the need to retain for our enforcement officers the ability themselves, in the course of their enforcement duties, to use devices which otherwise are illegal in this country, so that they may have such mechanical devices available to them as will assist them to the highest degree possible in the performance of their duty in the protection of law and order generally and, therefore, the protection of our democratic society. That this bill endeavours to do. It endeavours to do it in a way which retains the political responsibility which requires that applications for any such use by law enforcement officers be on the responsibility of an elected person, either the Solicitor General in the case of federal operations or, in by far the greater number of cases, the provincial attorneys general who have the general obligation of supervising police activity and the enforcement of the criminal law throughout this country.
I emphasize this, because it is not a matter of us as members of the government saying that you can rely in every way, in terms of political responsibility, upon us to do our job as individuals or persons. We are saying that we ought to be able, in this democratic process, in the provinces and in the federal government to rely on the political responsibility of the properly elected officials. I am indebted to the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester
Protection of Privacy
North for having said that that is the key to the proper operation of our system.
We are here saying we must rely upon the political responsibility of the provincial attorneys general for the greater part of the operation of this bill, that is, on the question of how many times and how frequently such applications or uses of these devices are in fact made. We do, of course, include reporting provisions so that we in advance attempt to put into the political process some ability such as may be reasonable and consistent with the use of the devices themselves with the power to control, supervise and see whether or not the devices are being used in a proper way. I will be eager in the committee to consider with members ways to improve and strengthen this ability to ensure that political control is really there in terms of the supervision by the Solicitor General, or by the provincial attorneys general, of the applications for these devices.
We make clear in the bill that these devices are not to be used as standard devices even by our law enforcement officers, but only when other techniques have been tried and failed or are unlikely to succeed. In other words, they are available as a fail-back position. That we do because we think they have obligations associated with them; they are evidence-gatherers which gather evidence beyond the matter that may be at hand in the law enforcement itself. In the bill we suggest a judge. We had initially said a judge of the superior court. The committee, when deliberating last year, added judges of the country court because of the concern that there should be access to judges by the police and by law enforcement agencies when they need quick action by a judge.
Some hon. members have suggested it would be better if we did not have a judge at all and relied totally on the political responsibility. I think it is better, in fact, to have it as we do, with the political responsibility in terms of the application proceeding and then, admittedly, a pro forma check-which may be all it can be in many cases because it is on an ex parte application-on the procedure by a judge. I think that could be helpful. I do not wish to go to any current or neighbouring cases to indicate when or how it could be helpful, but I think it could be and I shall be glad to pursue that matter further with the committee. Members of the opposition have suggested it would be better if a judge were not involved in that situation. Members opposite have suggested it.

speechtext: Not me.

speechtext:
I am happy to hear the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) say it was not him. Nor, indeed, I think, was it the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) whom I want to thank for his very kind intervention in the debate this afternoon. He attached great importance to the intervention of a judge in this process. He was very critical of the existence in the bill of the emergency permit which could be applied for by and on the responsibility of the Solicitor General or a provincial attorney general alone. So he is clearly on the side of wanting a judge to be involved. I am quite content to discuss that matter further and reach a conclusion in the committee as we try to come forward with the best possible bill.

May 8, 1973
Protection of Privacy
However, I would like to say, in answer to the remarks of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, that emergency permits may be necessary. I could say that generally about the need for the police authorities to use these devices in certain circumstances. There may be cases when it will come to the attention of an enforcement agency that there is apt to be soon some major criminal activity. Let us say, for instance, that it comes to their attention that there is a possibility that a significant shipment of heroin is about to be brought into this country. They may know by whom, but they may not know when. They may want to use a device like this, in such circumstances, quickly to determine the "when" in order to stop the import of the drug with all the terrible effects which can flow therefrom.
It may well be that in certain circumstances a judge is not available in time and that the emergency provisions in section 178.15 of the bill should be used. I draw to the attention of hon. members, again, that here too we have put in a political safeguard, not only that the application must be authorized by someone specifically authorized for the purpose by the Solicitor General, or by an attorney general, but there must also be reports upon the uses of such emergency permits so that they will be open to later examination and questioning about the extent to which they have been used.
What we cannot know at this stage is the extent of organized crime, whether it be related to drugs, kidnapping or hijacking, and whether it be national or international in scope, where our enforcement officers may need to have every mechanical device available to them in support of law and order in our society. It is there that I hope members of the committee will seriously consider the obligation to leave it open for our enforcement officers to have such devices as are ordinarily illegal in this country when it is necessary for them to have them in the course of apprehending or detecting serious criminal activity.
The same principle applies, of course, to the major crimes of sabotage and treason. There has been comment about the exact wording of the section referring to subversive activity. I will be very happy to consider that question with hon. members, and the nature of the words which should be in the section in order to provide adequate scope to deal with situations we cannot now foresee and at the same time properly to protect against the abuse of the use of these devices. There is, of course, still the political responsibility, and there too we can look at the question of whether we can strengthen the way in which political control is available if devices are used in that particular area.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members have generally agreed that the subject matter of this bill is important. It goes now to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I look forward to the resolution there, once again, by hon. members who compose this House of Commons of some of these key issues and the prompt return to the House and passage into law of this very important piece of legislation.
