speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment) moved
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
that Bill C-131, respecting wildlife in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-131 deals in relatively simple and straightforward terms with a very important subject, the protection and wise management of the wild living resources in this country. We have not had a wildlife act in Canada. We have had several pieces of legislation which have been used to manage our wild living resources reasonably well, but we need more comprehensive legislation to protect endangered species and to permit the federal government to purchase lands and manage the wildlife on those lands in a truly effective manner.
As most hon. members know, the management of most kinds of wildlife is a responsibility of the provincial government. The management of migratory birds is an exception. There is the Migratory Birds Convention Act, for example, which has been used very extensively by the Canada Wildlife Service in order to protect ducks, geese, seagulls, etc. Otherwise, the protection and wise management of wildlife in Canada has either been provincial in nature or as a result of co-operation between the federal government and the provinces, with the federal government frequently providing the research support, equipment, land and management techniques but with provincial law being used almost exclusively-that is, with the exception of the Migratory Birds Convention Act-for the safeguarding of wildlife in general.
Wild living things in many ways may be referred to as our first line of defence against pollution. There are many species of wild living things which are much more vulnerable to toxic substances, exceptional quantities of waste, and so on, than the human animal is, and when we see wildlife being destroyed we get our first inkling that we, as another living species on this planet, may be in trouble. But the protection of wild living things is important for another reason. It must be a determined objective of all levels of government, of all individuals and of all organizations in this country to preserve as much variety in nature as we possibly can. This is one of the several purposes, I would suggest-perhaps the most important purpose-which can be served by a Canada wildlife act such as is envisaged in Bill C-131.
I have mentioned legislation which has been used in the past, such as the Migratory Birds Convention Act. I could also have mentioned the Financial Administration Act. In fact, lands have been purchased, usually outright, by the federal government, or wildlife habitat sometimes have been gifted to the federal government, sometimes pur-
May 8, 1973

chased by the provinces or purchased co-operatively by the federal government and the provinces. But in the cases where the federal government has purchased these lands, under existing legislation it has not had the power, for example, to forbid private individuals entrance to those lands and obviously to protect certain species, particularly protect those which are now relatively scarce. It is essential, at least at times, to in effect insulate these lands from human activity or guard it from undue exploitation by curious visitors. This shortcoming, this inability under the federal law at least to properly manage lands will be overcome by the passage of this legislation.
There is another important aspect. It is important, I believe, from both the parliamentary point of view and the budgetary point of view. It is preferable to use legislation passed explicitly by this House, such as the Canada wildlife act, in order to defend the raising and spending of public moneys, rather than to use a more general piece of legislation such as the Financial Administration Act. In other words, parliament, should it pass Bill C-131, will give proper, full and explicit authority to the government of the day to spend moneys on, for example, research or demonstration projects, for the purchase of lands upon which wildlife can live and be protected, in which indeed it can be managed an 1 the populations expanded. In other words, the passage of this bill will give us a clear mandate from parliament to do a number of things which have been done under other legislation, and certain things which we have been unable to do under legislation passed previously.
I have mentioned the jurisdictional problem in many cases in respect of many species of wildlife, which is that the provincial power is paramount. However, provincial administrations usually rely on the Canadian Wildlife Service for advice and frequently look to the federal treasury for financial assistance. They often look to Ottawa for funds for the purchase of lands, not only for the management of bird life including migratory birds but animals and other kinds of wildlife as well.
The provinces are convinced that explicit support from parliament for legislation of this type, legislation which I hope will make additional funds available for the protection of wildlife, is highly desirable. There has been a history of not only co-operation, but in the last decade advocacy on the part of the provinces of a wildlife act at the federal level. Of course, many kinds of wildlife are interrelated in the normal ecological scheme of things. To manage one species in isolation is usually impossible, and of course for this reason a divided jurisdiction between Ottawa and the provinces has been awkward.
X10)
Beginning in 1961 at the Resources for Tomorrow Conference, a resolution was passed by the representatives of all levels of government recommending legislation of this kind. The Canadian Council of Resource Ministers in 1965 passed a resolution to the same effect. The bill now before hon. members has been discussed at length with all the provincial administrations responsible for recreation, conversation and protection of wildlife and is endorsed by all ten provincial administrations.
Protection of Wildlife
Essentially, this is a bill which, while it permits us to do certain things unilaterally in respect of migratory birds, generally envisages close co-operation with the provinces and in respect to other kinds of wildlife requires the federal government to consult closely with the provinces, and in many instances, unless there is a clear national involvement or concern, to obtain a positive recommendation from the provinces before, for example, buying land on which the management of wildlife can take place, land which is essential for the protection and preservation of a particular species.
There are four major aspects to the bill. The legislation will enable the federal government, (1) to acquire, control and manage lands for migratory bird conservation, interpretation and research. That is a federal responsibility. It will enable the federal government, (2) to acquire, control and manage lands for conservation and interpretation of and research on wildlife species other than migratory birds in co-operation with provincial and territorial governments.
It will enable the federal government, (3) to enter into co-operative arrangements with any province, territory, organization or person for matters of wildlife conservation, interpretation and research, and for the operation of lands and facilities related to wildlife resources, and (4) it will enable it to take any necessary action, in co-operation with provincial and territorial governments, required to protect endangered species of wildlife.
There are a number of species of wild living things in this great half continent of ours which are in serious difficulties. They have been wiped out over large parts of Canada. They include the cougar, the peregrine falcon and the bald eagle in the eastern half of the country, and the California big horn sheep, the whooping crane and the sea otter in the west. The latter which had been wiped out is now, hopefully, being re-established there. The survival of these species in this country is in many ways a matter of national concern and perhaps even a matter of continental and worldwide concern. That is one further reason for including a clause in this bill which relates to endangered species.
The Canadian Wildlife Service has performed many functions, has carried out a great deal of research and has done a great deal of work rehabilitating endangered species. For example, much of the pioneer work in respect of mercury was done by the Canadian Wildlife Service. It was picked up later by the federal fisheries service. The pioneer work done by the Canadian Wildlife Service had a lot to do with heading off a serious mercury problem, both in Canada and in the United States. Not only has the Canadian Wildlife Service carried out a great deal of research but it has published a great deal of informative material. Its personnel are well known. Many of them have international reputations. They have been responsible for a lot of the basic material which has been presented to the public through the media, television and otherwise. This is one of the reason why Canadians, relatively speaking, are well informed about wildlife in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer more specifically to the responsibilities of the Canadian Wildlife Service. With the passage of this legislation it will have control of all
3542

May 8, 1973
Protection of Wildlife
wildlife on public lands which have been purchased by or assigned to the government in general and the Department of the Environment in particular. At the request of other federal departments or agencies, the Canadian Wildlife Service will take charge of wildlife research, provide advice, establish facilities, and so on. The wildlife service will continue to act in an advisory capacity to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on the national parks, and more particularly will continue in its provincial-type responsibilities in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon.
Nothing in this legislation should be taken as restricting the rights of our Indian people except on those lands acquired by or assigned to the department by the governor in council. At the request of the Indian people, the Department of the Environment will continue to provide advice and assistance in developing and implementing measures for the wise use of wildlife resources on Indian lands.
Mr. Speaker, this is a short bill. It is a very important bill. I hope it will soon be referred to the standing committee. I know that hon. members will be very interested in many aspects of the Canadian Wildlife Service, in its plans for expansion and indeed in related plans of provincial departments and provincial administrations, plans which are often based on the findings and recommendations of the Canadian Wildlife Service. Our people in the department must be congratulated for the leadership they have shown in this very important field. I trust that this legislation will be passed promptly, because we at the federal level should be showing more leadership in this very important field.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members appreciate the thinking that has evolved over the years on the question of wildlife, its preservation and relationship to humanity and the web of life. Generally speaking, I believe the House welcomes Bill C-131

which gives a formal federal presence in this very important field of the preservation of endangered species and the control and management of our wildlife resources. I think it is exactly the same as Bill C-191 which was introduced last year and which died on the order paper, but we welcome its reappearance.
As the minister says, the main purpose of the bill is to enable the federal government to carry on what it has been doing under legislation, in a coherent manner with the co-operation of the provinces where that is essential. As the minister said, the care and preservation of wildlife lies primarily within provincial jurisdiction with the exception of migratory birds. In general, the bill is praiseworthy but it needs to be studied in the committee where suitable witnesses can be heard and where the purposes and the methods envisaged can be more carefully explained.
In the past there has been a lack of realization that humanity itself is part of the web of life. Throughout the world in general, even in Canada, we have been experiencing a population explosion of the human species. The balance of nature, if you like, has been upset and the detrimental effect of this imbalance on other species has been accentuated by the fact that the human species is by far the most destructive of the general environment of every species of life there is on this planet, earth.
The destruction of the environment by humans, of course, not only affects humanity's prospects in the future and the quality of life which will be available to it, but it affects other species as well. If any other species suffer extinction this, of course, is detrimental to the quality of life which is available to man. For example, in many areas of the country where certain species of wildlife formerly existed they are no longer found. I think we should not be satisfied with the objective of preventing the extinction in the whole country of the species, but where practical a habitat should be maintained for as many species as possible in as widespread an area of the country as possible.
In my little province of Prince Edward Island many species that were indigenous to the area have been extinct for perhaps a century, such as black bears, bobcats, etc. Unfortunately, in some cases they have been replaced by species introduced by man which are less desirable, such as skunks and racoons which were not native to Prince Edward Island to begin with.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to take much time on this bill because I think the House generally approves of it. I want to commend the minister on the concept of dealing with the provinces in the case of endangered species. As he said, some species that were unique to Canada have been exterminated-the type of walrus that existed in the Gulf of St. Lawrence at one time, for example, and various types of flightless birds which existed in Newfoundland, and there are endangered species such as the Ipswich sparrow whose only habitat is Sable Island.
It is important to preserve these species unique to Canada, but it is also important to preserve species which are endangered in Canada but which may exist in other places and to try to retain species in danger of becoming extinct in some parts of the country where their continuation might be practical. I must confess that I had a special
May 8, 1973

thrill four or five years ago, if I may use a personal incident, when I went for a walk in the woods in winter and found the track of an otter. This mammal was thought to be extinct in Prince Edward Island for many, many years but apparently there are a few survivors.
I think it is sad for Canada when we find that there are fewer whooping cranes, for example, in the whole country than there are Liberals in the House of Commons! I think that is unfortunate, if I may mix metaphors on both scores.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
No; for more whooping cranes. I want to say a few words about migratory birds. It has long been recognized that due to their habit, migratory birds are the special responsibility of the federal government and come under the international treaty on migratory birds. In the first instance, migratory birds were thought of chiefly as game birds. Then, of course, concern for birds which had little economic value, such as the whooping crane, came into the concept.
However, I think that as far as the future quality of life in many parts of the country is concerned, more consideration should be given to other types of migratory birds whose chief value is the pleasure they give to people living in a given environment. I do not mean just bird watchers, but people who live almost anywhere and enjoy migratory songbirds living in the same environment. In this regard I think there is perhaps a tendency for government, in trying to take action, to say, "We must acquire the habitat; we must have complete and full control over it". There is a place for that sort of approach, of course. However, I think there may also be a place for another concept under which the federal or provincial governments, acting singly or jointly, could procure easements on privately-owned property in cases where that property happens to be a remaining remnant of a suitable habitation for some type of migratory bird.
I know of woodlots in Prince Edward Island, which are small and are being decimated in many cases, which are the habitat of thrushes. I am sure that if those habitats were destroyed, the birds would be destroyed. In a few exceptional cases of this sort thought should be given to arrangements being entered into between owners of private property and governments so that the habitat of the wildlife concerned will not be destroyed. Some small rental might be paid, for instance, for preserving the habitat in its present form, or similar arrangements might be entered into.
Generally, I commend the minister for the bill. It is not a controversial one. I hope it lives up to the expectations that we all have for it. When the bill goes to committee it will be further studied and there will be a further determination of what can be expected of it.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-131, an act respecting wildlife in Canada, is legislation which is welcomed by our NDP group and will receive our support on second reading. This legislation is long overdue and will be acceptable to most conservation
Protection of Wildlife
groups in Canada. Many Canadians are surprised to find that although we have had a Canadian wildlife department for many years, there has never been a Canada wildlife act on our statute books.
Bill C-131 again outlines a major problem facing Canadians in the constitutional field. It clearly shows the trouble we are having in an area where there is mixed jurisdiction. This is probably the main reason for this legislation coming in at such a late date. Wildlife resources are primarily under provincial jurisdiction and, while the federal authorities have been co-operating for years in various undertakings, this legislation will tidy up federal operations and I trust will lead to increasing joint ventures with the provinces in wildlife research and conservation.
The section of the bill dealing with agreements between the federal and the provincial governments also includes possible agreements with municipal authorities, organizations and individuals on wildlife research, conservation and interpretation programs and measures. This is a most important feature of the legislation and could result in real benefit to our wildlife resource if carried out in an imaginative and co-operative manner. It could cover a host of projects both large and small, and be a real vehicle in the conservation fight going on throughout the country.
Another interesting aspect of the legislation is that which deals with public participation in wildlife conservation plans. I feel the success of any measures in the wildlife field will depend largely upon the understanding, co-operation and general knowledge of the Canadian public. The legislation indicates that the minister may undertake, promote or recommend measures for the encouragement of public co-operation in wildlife conservation and interpretation. This dissemination of information to the general public can be brought about by initiating conferences and meetings on the problems facing us in the wildlife field.
The legislation indicates that the minister may undertake programs for wildlife research and investigation and establish and maintain laboratories and other necessary facilities for that purpose. It also indicates that advisory committees may be appointed to advise the department on programs and policy. I feel this is a very important aspect of dealing successfully with wildlife conservation problems and trust that something meaningful will come out of this attempt to actively involve the general public in our over-all conservation plans. There is no doubt about the growing interest of Canadians generally in wildlife conservation, and I am pleased to see that an effort will be made to not only promote the need for wildlife conservation but also to utilize the vast amount of practical knowledge which can be contributed by many Canadians who are experts in this field.
May I again bring to the attention of the minister a suggestion which I have raised many times in the House of Commons. It deals with the setting up of an environmental council which is wholly independent of government. The council would report upon environmental problems throughout the country. It would report, without fear or favour, its findings in the environmental field. It would have adequate research facilities and should be in a position to examine government policies, or lack of them, and
3544

May 8, 1973
Protection of Wildlife
to indicate where changes should be made. It would be able to propose courses of action and outline areas where priority measures were required and where immediate action should be taken. It would, naturally, deal with many aspects of wildlife conservation and could give guidance to government and the general public alike as to the measures and the cost involved to meet the ever increasing challenge to our valuable wildlife resource.
There is another serious problem facing wildlife conservationists not only in Canada but in practically every country in the world. That is the need to protect endangered species. For too many years governments at all levels have neglected to adequately protect the environment until we have reached the stage where a very large number of animals and birds are on the verge of extinction as a result of our activities. The protection of endangered species is a very complex problem. It involves not only man's encroachment on wildlife habitat and his unwise cropping of certain species, but it involves primarily man's activity in the economic field. We have used the air, the land and the water as receptacles for effluents which come from our factories and industries. Massive amounts of pesticides have been used without adequate research being done to know if they could be safely used. As a result there is an increasing number of endangered wildlife species to be found everywhere, and Canada is no exception.
Some steps have been taken to rectify this situation, but far more money must be poured into research than ever before and more stringent measures must be used to enforce strict environmental controls if these endangered species are to survive. Time is of the essence and I suggest to the minister that this is one of the priorities in the wildlife field. Through man's economic activities we are endangering the very existence of a number of species. It must be obvious that man himself is in danger, for we depend upon similar food chains in our environment for continued existence.
Other members of our group, Mr. Speaker, will be dealing with specific aspects of the legislation currently being debated. Before closing I would like to speak briefly about the wildlife service which will be administering this legislation. There are a number of highly qualified individuals in the wildlife service. I trust the passage of this bill will indicate that the minister intends to increase the staff of this service so that it can adequately handle the many problems facing it in various parts of Canada.
I would first draw to the attention of the minister the lack of full and proper ecological studies being carried out in our Canadian Arctic. We are all aware that certains studies are being carried out by various government departments, chiefly in connection with the proposed oil and gas pipelines from the north. While some useful information will certainly come from these studies, most of them are crash programs designed to test the feasibility of pipelines down the Mackenzie valley. Competent biologists feel that we still have no adequate program of publicly-sponsored fundamental research. This type of research is essential as it will determine the baselines of an ecological system and would assist us in predicting what stresses can or cannot be placed upon it.

I would point out to the minister that most of the current research is going on in the Mackenzie River valley. There are other areas in the north which have never been touched and where there is great need of environmental research of all types. All Canadians know the increasing economic activity being carried on in the north, and I suggest there should be no further delay by any department of government in getting the basic research started for the whole of our valuable northern territories. It will take many years to complete, but it will assist us to avoid the many mistakes which have already been made in several parts of our Arctic territory.
In the report released just over a year ago by the Environmental Protection Board, a so-called independent body of experts, it was stated that Canada's level of ecological research in the Arctic was abysmally low. Their work was carried on primarily in the Mackenzie River valley where, as I previously stated, a number of environmental surveys have been made or are currently going on. If the environmental and ecological research in that area is classed as abysmally low, then it is obvious that the rest of the north continues to be virtually ignored.
I understand that under the department there is the Canadian Wildlife Service's Arctic ecology unit. It was established primarily to monitor how northern activity affects wildlife and to isolate wildlife areas needing special protection. This Arctic ecology unit was set up in 1970 but up until a year ago at least it was a one-man affair. According to a report made by Pollution Probe, in Toronto, in April of last year the scientist in this unit has been so busy keeping an eye on oil companies and their seismic and drilling operations that he has not had much chance to do any short-term let alone long-range ecological studies.
I remind the minister that the complete unit was originally intended to comprise 12 men, which would be the minimum number required to start a proper research program. These individuals must be highly specialized in order to set up and carry out the type of research which is urgently required by Canada in our Arctic areas. I would ask the minister if any additional staff has been added to the Arctic ecology unit this year, and why he has been so slow in staffing this extremely important research unit. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, this bill will help to provide the necessary funds for this type of research which is especially required. May I again urge that priority attention be given to this matter.
This research in the Arctic is closely tied in with this wildlife bill. I am fully aware of the conflicting jurisdiction in the north in so far as both the territorial councils and other federal departments are concerned. On a number of occasions I have pointed out and protested the real lack of authority which the Department of the Environment has over environmental affairs as far as the north is concerned. The chief federal administrative body in the north is the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and there is no doubt that the Department of the Environment plays a very secondary role even where matters of conservation are concerned. I consider this a major weakness in our federal environmental administrative structure. It should be corrected.
May 8, 1973

The need for additional skilled staff in our Arctic ecology unit might be best illustrated by the greatly increased oil and gas mineral exploration which is going on in our Arctic areas. The program is accelerating and there is increasing urgency for basic ecological research to be carried out and evaluated before immense damage is done to our Arctic ecology.
I believe the following quotation from a paper delivered at the Twentieth Alaska Science Conference in 1969 by R. A. Hemstock, the Arctic co-ordinator for Imperial Oil Ltd., clearly outlines the needs of the oil industry in our Arctic areas as of that date. He said:
In summary, the 470,000 square miles of potential oil lands in the Canadian Arctic will require for development: (a) Extensive geological reconnaissance; (b) reconnaissance and detailed geophysical surveys for a total of 150,000 miles; (c) drilling of 700-1400 exploratory and 6,000-12,000 development wells for petroleum; (d) construction of 4,000 miles of access roads and 4,000 miles of trunk roads based on northern Canada experience of 1 mile of road per well; (e) construction of 8,000 miles of gathering pipelines and many miles of large trunk lines to market or to marine terminals; (f) construction of camp, town, airfields and sport facilities for an additional population of 10,000 oil workers.
This is only part of the program of northern economic development and I have dealt with it in a very general manner. I trust, however, that the Canada wildlife act will be the instrument by which a federal government can initiate research, not only in Arctic areas but in every part of our country, to ensure that future generations will be able to enjoy the wonderful wildlife resource which nature has given to Canadians in abundance and which it is our duty as legislators to try to protect for future generations. In closing, I intend to support the bill on second reading, as will other members of the New Democratic Party.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my party has been accused on a number of occasions of not being constructive in respect of legislation. I do not accept that charge. On this occasion I take great pleasure in supporting this bill. I take a personal interest in this bill because in many respects I feel it is the culmination of the life of a member of my family. The chief migratory birds officer for western Canada during the twenties and thirties devoted his life to the objective that this bill is outlining. I spent many summers in his home, where I saw gathering together that collection of species and other variances which on his death James Alexander Munro gave, and which now reposes in the National Museum of Canada at the foot of Metcalfe Street here in Ottawa. Tribute was paid to him in the form of a plaque. I am very pleased to be able to pay tribute in this House to his memory.
There are other features of the bill with which I should like to deal. I have two comments to make, and I shall be brief. I feel that at last, through clauses 3(b) and 3(e) taken together, the federal authority will have the power to eliminate what is sometimes described as an inhumane trap. I do not know quite what the correct word would be; "inhumane" is not exactly the right word unless we go into anthropomorphology. Perhaps "inanimal" would be a more appropriate adjective. I refer to the claw trap which was used during part of our development.
Protection of Wildlife
Now, happily, a new type of trap has been developed in connection with the economic management of the wildlife of our country. It is known as the conibear trap and it permits the taking of animals for their fur in a manner which does not injure the animal to the same extent. The old claw trap which we sometimes used when we were younger, when we lived on the prairies, and which we used to trap gophers and other small animals caused excruciating pain and lingering death to these helpless creatures. Man is able to fend for himself, and he does so, but wildlife is not so fortunate in an environment inhabited or frequented by humans. Therefore, as a mark of civilization I feel we should take certain responsibilities upon ourselves.
In many respects the legislation now brought forward will enable the authorities of this country to protect and manage our resources upon the basis of which, let us not forget it, this country developed. Canada developed through the fur trade and we still profit by the fur trade. But let us accept modern developments in the management of that trade. I believe clauses 3(b) and 3(e) will enable federal and provincial authorities to insist that these resources are carefully controlled not only for economic reasons, the value in dollars produced, but because of their environmental impact.
We hear so much these days about the quality of life. Those of us who have time at this time of the year and a little later in the year might be happy to go out in some of the parks around here and see a phenomenon on which our country stands and has stood from its very beginning-the beavers building their dams. This is one of the delights which those of us who have become overurbanized often forget. Let us not destroy such pleasures. Let us remember that they can be preserved.
My other comment concerns clause 9. I suppose this particular clause was aimed at preserving those migratory animals which spend part of the year in Canada, and I am delighted to see that with shrewd judgment it can be used to do even more. I asked a question in the House on April 16 which hon. members will find reported at page 3328 of Hansard. It concerned the importation into Canada of the pelts of endangered species from Mexico, Brazil and other exotic lands. It was my understanding that some of these pelts were imported into Canada because of the ease with which they could enter this country due to the nature of our tariff policies and our customs regulations. The minister indicated in his reply that Environment Canada had taken a leading role in international discussions on this subject.
Clause 9 will enable those discussions to be even more fruitful and will help prevent this sort of thing happening. I have seen some of the statistics published in the papers concerning the numbers of pelts brought into this country for reshipment to other countries where they can be made into fancy jackets and fancy long coats. This involves the pelts of species which are endangered in the exotic lands. They are noble creatures whose preservation we must seek, and I am happy to see that facilities to ensure such preservation exist in the legislation before us.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE RECIPIENTS IN NURSING HOMES-SUGGESTED PROTECTION OF PORTION OF PENSIONS AGAINST RISING RATES
SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE RECIPIENTS IN NURSING HOMES-SUGGESTED PROTECTION OF PORTION OF PENSIONS AGAINST RISING RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 29 I addressed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) concerning the increase in rent imposed upon senior citizens subsequent to, or indeed in some cases prior to the increase in old age security pension payments. The question as it appears in Hansard makes reference to a recent proposal from a number of very prestigious deliberative bodies. This is actually an error. What I referred to was a member of a very prestigious body, namely, the Senate of Canada, referred to frequently in this chamber as the other place. This is an expression whose procedural antecedents are difficult to trace.
Since the question was raised by myself and other members of the House we have heard a statement from the Minister of State responsible for housing (Mr. Basford) to the effect that he had disseminated his views to the proprietors of institutions under federal responsibility-I presume directly or indirectly.
There are many institutions across the land, operated by provincial governments, which have in fact received considerable assistance, as far as their construction is concerned, from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It would seem to me that the concern for the kind of practices to which this question refers may properly be expressed by the Government of Canada because of its practical and helpful involvement through CMHC.
I hope the parliamentary secretary or whoever will reply to me tonight will be able to indicate what has been the outcome of representations made by the minister directly responsible for reporting for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and what his own minister has been able to do in the field of moral suasion.
The plight of our senior citizens is a most serious one, Mr. Speaker. Today's shocking statistics on the rapidly accelerating cost of living, particularly in the field of food

at home and housing, should cause grave anxiety to anyone who has concern for the welfare and well-being of the senior citizens of Canada. Indeed, the past decade has constituted a painful assault upon the security of the aged, on those on fixed income and certainly on those in the low and middle-income range.
As I pointed out when I spoke at the time of the introduction of the amendment to the Old Age Security Act, we have been literally taking it out on the older people because they have borne, without adequate relief, the debilitating burden of runaway inflation. As I pointed out, had the actual cost of living been added to the old age security pensions from 1963 on, the figure would be slightly less than $107. Therefore, the increase to $100, while certainly better than the addition of 42 cents a month which was considered adequate before October 30, is in fact something a good deal less than a burst of generosity or a real solution to the struggle of our senior citizens to cope with the reality of today's inflated living costs.
I have reason to believe, from correspondence which I have received from all across the country, that they are again being subjected to new hikes in their rent so great as to leave them really no better off than they were before the passage of the amendment to the Old Age Security Act. I had a letter not long ago from a lady living in a provincially-operated senior citizens' home, or unit, who told me that her rent was to be increased, effective in June, from $46 per month to $102. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what this sort of increase will do to the life pattern, the life style of a Canadian who has contributed to this our country for decades and who now seeks to live out her closing years with some degree of security and some relief from the anxiety of financial burdens!
It is a sad commentary on our present-day government that while its spokesman in this field, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, can talk of programs of a long-range nature-three, four and five years-the same minister can have such difficulty in grappling with the immediate needs of our senior citizens. The same, indeed, could be said about those who are not senior citizens. What a help it would be if the new family allowance legislation proposal could be put into legislation immediately and a contribution thereby given to many of our people with families who just cannot provide the basic needs of food and shelter for their children. But the earliest on this from the government seems to be January 1, 1974.
The latest figures of the cost of living index have already eroded the increase which the senior citizens received in their April cheques. Something must be done about this. We cannot continue to allow these people to be victimized. A way must be found to protect the senior citizens of this country from further threats to their economic and financial security.
We now use the expression "old age security". Once it was called an old age pension. The newer expression is more euphoneous and perhaps more pleasing. But there is not much security involved if, when the present government provides even a meagre increase-and the most recent pension increase was a meagre one-somebody else immediately takes away the benefit of that increase which the Parliament of Canada voted. This is a shameful, dis-
May 8, 1973

turbing, distressing, unpleasant and unnecessary situation. I would suggest that careful thought be given to this matter and that in this day of gnawing, nagging, terrible increases in the cost of living a way be found to translate the concern of this House-I trust the House is concerned-into meaningful action to protect such security as our older citizens have the right to expect.

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE RECIPIENTS IN NURSING HOMES-SUGGESTED PROTECTION OF PORTION OF PENSIONS AGAINST RISING RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and the members of this House share the hon. member's concern for the pensioner in this situation, though the rising cost of living presents problems to persons on limited incomes whether or not they are in nursing homes. The federal government has actively encouraged the provinces and has provided financial support under the Canada Assistance Plan to supplement the incomes of pensioners and others who are unable to maintain themselves in relation to their needs.
Under CAP agreements, all provinces provide financial assistance to residents of nursing homes and other types of homes for special care as required to meet their individual costs of maintenance. Federal contributions for this purpose exceed $150 million annually. Other provisions of the agreement concern the shared-cost comforts allowance which the resident may spend as he wishes, as it need not be applied to the regular cost of care.
We must remember that prior to federal cost-sharing many welfare institutions had no comforts allowances. It is encouraging to find more of them now. An approach used by two provinces to date is to cover specified health care costs in nursing homes under provincial health insurance. The resident then pays only a fixed portion of the cost toward the residential cost. Such costs are within the capability of most OAS pensioners and do not fluctuate automatically each time the pension is increased.
The hon. member should know that Ontario has just raised the basic rate from $3.50 per day to $4.00 per day in spite of the federal government's expressed wish that the rate not be increased at the time the pension was increased to $100. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) instructed the authorities in homes under the jurisdiction of CMHC that no such raises would be approved. Finally, it does not appear to be a situation where federal legislation is appropriate, as the matter is clearly under provincial jurisdiction.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATION TO INCREASE BASIC RATE OF DISABILITY PENSION
VETERANS AFFAIRS-INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATION TO INCREASE BASIC RATE OF DISABILITY PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) in the few months he has been in his portfolio has established a good record and has won the confidence of all of us in this House who are interested in the welfare of our veterans. He has to his credit the piloting through this House of a bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. He also has to his credit the fact that he has made clear to the members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs that he supports the report of the joint study group on the basic rate of the war disability pension.
Adjournment Debate
However, Sir, I confess I am beginning to feel a bit of concern over the time it is taking for the minister to bring to this House a bill to amend the Pension Act to implement the report of that joint study group. I therefore use this "late show" period tonight to raise the matter, not to heap criticism on the minister's head but to let him know that he has the support of this entire House with regard to this matter and also to let him know that we want him to persuade his cabinet colleagues to let him bring in that bill without further delay.
The fact is that on Tuesday, January 9, as recorded in Hansard at pages 88 and 89, the minister said that the report of the joint study group would soon be referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. He kept his word. This was done on Thursday, February 15, as recorded at page 1322 of Hansard.
On Friday, February 23, as reported in Hansard at page 1585, the standing committee reported back to the House indicating its endorsation of the recommendation in the report of the joint study group. In the meantime, on Monday, February 19, as recorded in Hansard at page 1432, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) had indicated that the government was simply waiting, so far as war disability pensions were concerned, for the report of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
On Friday, March 16, as recorded in Hansard at page 2298, the minister assured me that the legislation would be forthcoming soon. When Wednesday, April 4, came along and it still had not appeared I asked him again, as recorded in Hansard at page 2968, whether we might expect it soon and in particular whether he would try to get it before us before Easter. The minister said that he would try to do so.
However, yesterday, with the Easter recess now over, I questioned the minister again and to my regret he was not able to make quite such a positive statement as to when this bill might come in. If the delay is because the minister is having trouble getting his cabinet colleagues to agree to a recommendation that calls for the basic rate to be tied to certain categories within the public service, I am prepared for him to take a little longer to win that principle. What we do not want is for him to bring in just a dollar figure that leaves unresolved the matter that veterans have been fighting for for 50 years.
This is an extremely important matter. I know the minister's heart and mind are in the right place, and if the trouble he is having is inside that cabinet I hope he can let his fellow ministers know that this House is on his side. Indeed, I ask him to draw the cabinet's attention to an editorial in the May issue of The Legion, the monthly magazine of the Royal Canadian Legion, entitled "Keeping the Faith". The first part of the editorial commends the minister, the government and the opposition on what was done with respect to improvements in the War Veterans Allowance Act. But then the editorial says this:
We hope the government will soon give evidence of its awareness of a similar responsibility to Canada's war disability pensioners by the establishment of a basic rate tied to an index of salary schedules for unskilled workers in the public service. The joint study group report recommending such a basic rate of pension has been given unanimous approval by the parliamentary committee

May 8, 1973
Adjournment Debate
on veterans affairs and now awaits action by the government in the form of a bill amending the Pension Act. In the past, increases in disability pension rates were nearly always announced simultaneously with increases in war veterans allowances. Consequently disability pensioners are getting concerned about the lack of any announcement of the government's intentions, particularly since their pensions are based on a very special relationship which exists where the individual has served his country and in return was given assurance that compensation would be paid.
I am sure that the sentiment of that paragraph reflects the thinking of the House. I am sure, also, it reflects the thinking of the minister. It is an excellent report that was produced by the joint study group. The Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs was behind it 100 per cent and so is this House. But I hope the minister will soon be able to say that he has won the battle of his life with the cabinet and that he will be able to bring in a bill that relates the basic rate of the war disability pension to selected salary schedules in the public service so that war disability pensioners in the future will not, as they have over the years, slid behind year after year. The minister has our full support and we hope he will give us the right answer soon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATION TO INCREASE BASIC RATE OF DISABILITY PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will, of course, not expect me to make any announcement of new policy at this time. I would, however, remind the House that the report on basic rates of pensions was prepared by a joint working group comprised of government officials and of representatives of veterans' organizations. The government has the whole subject under active consideration, and I have already indicated that I shall be happy to inform the House in further detail when I am in a position to do so. I expect this to be quite soon.
I should emphasize that the government has been keeping the Pensions Act, like other items of the veterans' charter, under regular review. Two years ago the government introduced and parliament enacted amendments which were the result of the most thorough review of the Pension Act in the past 50 years.
Just last year at about this time the government introduced budget measures which provided for the automatic increase of pensions in line with changes in the cost of living. Pursuant to this legislation, pensions were increased by 3.6 per cent effective January 1 of this year. A further automatic increase can be expected next January. It will therefore be clear that the government has continued to recognize and fulfil its responsibility under the veterans' charter and I assure the House that we will continue to do so.

subtopic: HEALTH-STATUS OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON PROVISION OF CHRONIC CARE IN NURSING HOMES
HEALTH-STATUS OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON PROVISION OF CHRONIC CARE IN NURSING HOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak of the need for chronic care nursing homes and on the necessity for people who have to go to those homes to be included under OHIP the same as if they went to acute treatment beds in hospital. A witch hunt is being made for someone to blame for rising health costs. There is negligence at both levels of government in not seeing that beds for the chronically ill are available. My sympathy has always gone out to the ill, many of them decrepit, mental-

ly depressed and unable to help themselves. It is for this reason that I am not impressed with the fencing of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and his provincial counterparts. It is surely the responsibility of the federal government to see that health care is universal across Canada.
That health care costs are getting out of control needs no comment; it is a fact. Citadels of medical teaching and training continue to accord a low priority to the dire need for education in this field. The increased care in and the mounting costs of general hospitals make it imperative for chronic disease hospitals to cope with many complex problems. There should be established fellowship training programs in geriatric medicine, all in the setting of a chronic disease hospital.
How do we reduce the length of stay in hospital? The first thing is to keep people out of hospital. This means that we must have proper facilities in chronic care nursing homes so that patients can be discharged from hospital. Bottlenecks are occurring in hospitals. In my own hospital, bottlenecks are occurring now where people have applied for chronic nursing home care but are still waiting.
Who is going to build the needed chronic care nursing homes? Surely it is the responsibility of the federal government and provincial governments to see that funds are available for private organizations to build them. This should be part of the medicare program and should be shared equally with the federal government.
We can reduce the length of hospital stay by practising preventive medicine and preventing long, disabling illness by treating it before it becomes firmly established. This means that we must have sufficient doctors to do general practice and enough to practice preventive medicine before the illness becomes either acute, or results in a hospital case.
Many people today who are going to the emergency departments of hospitals could in many cases be treated in doctor's offices. Probably only 25 per cent of those appearing in the emergency wards of hospitals today need that type of treatment. The rest could be equally well treated in doctors' offices. To do this it is necessary to obtain an adequate supply of doctors. Medical schools should be operated so that a doctor is graduated in four years instead of six years, which would reduce the overhead costs of graduating a doctor and have him earning money and paying income taxes approximately two years before he would with the horse and buggy course that most medical schools are following today and which are getting us into trouble.
McMaster University now graduates a doctor in three years and other schools in five years, but most in six years. The cost per doctor across Canada varies in many cases. Surely the grants from the federal government should be made specifically on a per capita basis in relation to the number of doctors graduated at the school. This would lead to far more efficiency. Reducing the time of the course would allow a doctor to be in practice two years earlier. It seems to me that a doctor could be given an interim certificate for a period of three to five years and
May 8, 1973

then sent to areas where a doctor is needed for general practice, which would cover a lot of regions in desperate need of doctors.
An incentive could be given to the doctor who goes into these areas by an income tax reduction or other means. You would then have a doctor with far more experience in general practice and of much more value if he became a specialist. He could make up his mind whether he would be a general practitioner and/or a specialist and, faced with these facts, would make a better choice.
Getting people out of hospital is simply one way in which extended care should be available to all patients capable of being discharged and the long wait by chronically ill patients for the necessary accommodation to become available would be reduced. This should be paid for on the same basis exactly as acute care. Both of these points are essential-to get people out of hospital and give them adequate care, and increase the availability of beds when they are ready to be discharged from active treatment hospital beds.
Mr. Speaker, the cost of chronic care or extended care is approximately one-quarter the cost of acute care in a hospital, of which one-quarter is paid by the old age pensions in a chronic care home. This will indicate the necessity of grappling with this problem and solving it in Canada. Surely it is not an insurmountable problem. It is very unfair for the minister and his provincial counterparts to be hunting all over for somebody to lay the blame on, when it is very simple: first you try to get them into hospital for adequate medical care; second, get them discharged as quickly as possible and have chronic care beds waiting. Hospitalization should cover both. Hospitalization and chronic care would cost roughly 25 per cent of

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: HEALTH-STATUS OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON PROVISION OF CHRONIC CARE IN NURSING HOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that a federal-provincial conference is being held today to arrive at such an agreement concerning health care costs and cost-sharing. He must know also that it is generally accepted that we must combat the rise in these costs.
A new financing formula was proposed to the provinces in January, and again today, under which payments are to be made on a per capita basis. The annual increase in costs are to be held down to the same level as the yearly GNP increase, rather than the present 13 per cent rate. This new agreement presents a change in emphasis, more toward a global budgeting concept, leaving the provinces the flexibility to decide how to apportion the funds according to the needs of their population. It is understood that basic standards of comprehensiveness, accessibility, universality and portability would have to be maintained.
I should like to add that preventive medicine is already a stated priority of the federal government. Emphasis, on the fitness side, of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the tripling of the fitness and sport budget in the next three years demonstrate this. Also, fitness, sport and recreation have been transferred to the health side of the department, echoing this change in emphasis.
We all share the hon. member's concern about the escalation in costs. We also realize that expensive hospital beds are not the solution. Finally, we hope for agreement from today's conference because the situation warrants immediate action by the federal government and also by the provincial governments.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.28 p.m.
